Question 1



Question 1




Show R code
# variance values 
V <- 2
W <- 1

# function for gt
gt <- function(t){
  (-1)^t/2
}

# initial values for the Normal distribution
m0 = 0 
C0 = 1

# function for ft as given 
Ft <- function(t){
  rnorm(1, 0.2)
}

# initialising vectors y, theta and f values for 100 observations
yt <- numeric(100)
theta <- numeric(100)
F_values <- numeric(100)

# first thea value mean
theta_previous <- rnorm(1, mean = m0, sd = sqrt(C0))

# loop for simulating latent gdp values and the observed values 
for (i in seq_len(100)) {
  F_values[i] <- Ft(i)

  theta[i] <- gt(i) * theta_previous +
    rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(W))

  yt[i] <- F_values[i] * theta[i] +
    rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(V))

  theta_previous <- theta[i]
}


In the code, theta[i] represents the underlying, unobserved state at time (i), while yt[i] represents the observed data. Random noise is included in both equations to account for process and measurement uncertainty. Process noise allows the underlying state to vary beyond what is explained by the state transition equation. Measurement noise represents variation in the observations around F_values[i] * theta[i], so the observations do not reveal the underlying state exactly.
The coefficient gt(i) determines how the previous hidden state contributes to the current state. In this model, it alternates between −0.5 and 0.5. The coefficient F_values[i] links the current hidden state to the observed data by multiplying theta[i]. Both coefficients vary over time.

2. Use the Kalman Filter for parameter estimation and to fit the model. Write your own code for the Kalman Filter, not using R package functions.
I used the one in the textbook as the template. I changed tweaked the function to not use the full vectors as the coefficients F and G are not constant but change with time.


Show R code
# function for the kalman filter
Kfilter <- function(FF, GG, m0, C0, W, V, y) {
N = length(y)
at = numeric(N + 1)
Rt = numeric(N + 1)
ft = numeric(N)
Qt = numeric(N)
mt = numeric(N)
Ct = numeric(N)
et = numeric(N)


## predict theta
at[1] = GG(1) * m0
Rt[1] = GG(1)^2* C0 + W

for (i in 1:N) {
## predict y
ft[i] = FF[i] * at[i]
Qt[i] = FF[i]^2 * Rt[i] + V
## posterior
if (is.na(y[i])) {
et[i] = 0
Kt = 0
} else {
Kt = Rt[i] *  FF[i]/Qt[i]
et[i] = y[i] - ft[i]
}
mt[i] = at[i] + Kt * et[i]
Ct[i] = Rt[i] - Kt * FF[i] * Rt[i]

## predict theta
at[i+1] = GG(i+1) * mt[i]
Rt[i+1] = GG(i+1)^2 * Ct[i] + W
}
return(list(at = at, Rt = Rt, ft = ft, Qt = Qt, mt = mt, Ct = Ct))
}

fitted_kf <- Kfilter(FF = F_values, GG = gt, m0 = m0, C0 = C0 , W = W, V = V, y = yt)


In the function the prediction error, et[i], is the difference between the observed and predicted values. It provides new information for updating our estimate of the hidden state. The Kalman filter adjusts the predicted state mean by Kt * et[i], where Kt is the Kalman gain and determines how the prediction error affects the update.
When measurement noise is high, the Kalman filter gives less weight to the observations when updating the state estimate. Holding the other quantities fixed, a larger measurement variance reduces the magnitude of the Kalman gain, so the filter relies more on its predicted state.
The function checks whether y[i] is missing. If it is, there is no observation available to update the predicted state, so the Kalman gain is set to zero. The updated state mean and variance therefore remain equal to their predicted values. This allows the Kalman filter to handle missing observations and continue predicting.


3. Forecast up to \(h = 5\), with prediction intervals.


Show R code
n <- length(yt)
h <- 5 # forecasting horison

# Missing future observations
y <- c(yt, rep(NA, times = h))

# Generate future observation coefficients
FF <- c(F_values, sapply((n + 1):(n + h), Ft))

fit <- Kfilter(
  FF = FF, GG = gt,
  m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = W, V = V, y = y
)

# conbined the actual y values, predicted and intervals as well
vals <- cbind(
  observed = y,
  predicted = fit$ft,
  lower = fit$ft - 1.96 * sqrt(fit$Qt),
  upper = fit$ft + 1.96 * sqrt(fit$Qt)
)

# plotting of the prediction invervals for the data 
plot_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(nrow(vals)),
  vals
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -time,
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "y"
  )

ggplot(plot_data, aes(time, y, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n + 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      observed = "black", predicted = "blue",
      lower = "grey", upper = "grey"
    ),
    breaks = c("observed", "predicted", "lower"),
    labels = c("observed", "predicted", "95% prediction limits")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "y", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1)
  )









Show R code
# Display the five forecasts
vals[(n + 1):(n + h), ]


     observed     predicted     lower    upper
[1,]       NA -0.3438910728 -5.234440 4.546658
[2,]       NA  0.0276190625 -2.828037 2.883275
[3,]       NA  0.0038262316 -2.774737 2.782389
[4,]       NA -0.0006857614 -2.773413 2.772041
[5,]       NA -0.0025715907 -2.822933 2.817790


The code below shows the appending of the 5 values because appending five missing values extends the observation vector to include the forecast horizon. At each future time point, the filter predicts the state and observation. Because the future observation is missing, it skips the observation update and carries the predicted state forward to generate the next forecast.
The predicted values show much less variation than the observed values and remain close to zero. This is because they represent the expected observations, while the actual observations include process and measurement noise. The observed values appear to fall within the 95% prediction limits. The vertical dashed line separates the observed period from the forecast period, which extends five time steps ahead.


4. Plot data with fitted and filtered level estimates.


Show R code
# Observation scale plot
observation_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  Observed = yt,
  `One-step fitted` = fitted_kf$ft,
  `Filtered observation` = F_values * fitted_kf$mt,
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -time,
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(observation_data, aes(time, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "black",
      "One-step fitted" = "blue",
      "Filtered observation" = "darkgreen"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "One-step fitted", "Filtered observation")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Observation", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









Show R code
# State scale plot
state_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  `True level` = theta,
  `Filtered level` = fitted_kf$mt,
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -time,
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(state_data, aes(time, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "True level" = "grey",
      "Filtered level" = "darkgreen"
    ),
    breaks = c("True level", "Filtered level")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Level", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









In the observation plot, the one-step fitted values (fitted_kf$ft, blue) use information from previous observations, while the filtered observation estimates (F_values * fitted_kf$mt, green) also incorporate the current observation. The green line generally follows the observed values more closely than the blue line. In the filter code, the state mean is updated using mt[i] = at[i] + Kt * et[i], so the Kalman gain determines how much the prediction error adjusts the estimate.
In the state plot, the filtered level (fitted_kf$mt, green) captures some movements in the true simulated level (theta, grey), but misses several peaks and troughs. This is because the hidden state is estimated from noisy observations rather than observed directly. Although the filter accounts for process and measurement uncertainty through W and V, it cannot perfectly separate the state from the noise, so uncertainty remains after the update.


5.Calculate the residuals and show an autocorrelation plot.


Show R code
# redisuals extracted 
residuals <- yt - fitted_kf$ft
# scaled 
standardised_residuals <- residuals / sqrt(fitted_kf$Qt)

# plot of residuals scaled
residual_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_along(standardised_residuals),
  residual = standardised_residuals
)

ggplot(residual_data, aes(x = time, y = residual)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = time, y = 0, yend = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Standardised residual") +
  theme_classic()









Show R code
# acf plot
acf(standardised_residuals,
    main = "ACF of standardised prediction residuals")









If the model captures the time dependence well, I would expect no significant autocorrelation in the standardised prediction residuals at non-zero lags. The ACF plot shows no significant spikes beyond lag 0, which supports this expectation and suggests that the model has adequately captured the time dependence. The spike at lag 0 is expected because each residual is perfectly correlated with itself.

Question 4
In this exercise, you will write your own code for updating regression coefficients using a Kalman filter. We will model quarterly growth rates in US personal consumption expenditure (\(y\)) against quarterly growth rates in US real personal disposable income (\(z\)). So the model is \(y_t = a + bz_t + e_t\).
The corresponding state space model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= a_t + b_t z_t + e_t,\\
a_t &= a_{t-1},\\
b_t &= b_{t-1}.
\end{aligned}
\] a) Plot the data (usconsumption[,1], usconsumption[,2]) and fit a linear regression model to the data using the lm function.


Show R code
# importing data, had to use ai to help me find the data because fpp does not exist anymore in R. 
data("uschange")
y <- uschange[, 1] # consumption 
z <- uschange[, 2] # disposable income
T_len <- length(y)


# making to a data fram to use for lm 
cons_data<- data.frame(
  time = as.numeric(time(y)),
  consumption = as.numeric(y),
  income = as.numeric(z)
)

# Linear regression
fit1 <- lm(consumption ~ income, data = cons_data)
summary(fit1)

The scatterplot shows a positive association between quarterly disposable income growth and consumption growth. Consumption growth tends to increase as income growth increases, with the fitted regression line making this trend clearer. However, the points show considerable spread around the line, indicating that income growth alone does not fully explain consumption growth. The vertical differences between the observed points and the fitted line are the regression residuals.

2. Write some R code to implement the Kalman filter using the above state space model.


Show R code
# used the textbook version but adjusted based on the dimensions 
Kfilter <- function(FF, GG, m0, C0, W, V, y) {
  N = length(y)
  p = length(m0)

  at = matrix(0, N + 1, p)
  Rt = array(0, dim = c(p, p, N + 1))
  ft = numeric(N)
  Qt = numeric(N)
  mt = matrix(0, N, p)
  Ct = array(0, dim = c(p, p, N))
  et = numeric(N)

  ## predict state
  at[1, ] = GG %*% m0
  Rt[, , 1] = GG %*% C0 %*% t(GG) + W

  for (i in seq_len(N)) {
    Fi = FF[i, , drop = FALSE]

    ## predict observation
    ft[i] = Fi %*% at[i, ]
    Qt[i] = Fi %*% Rt[, , i] %*% t(Fi) + V

    ## posterior
    if (is.na(y[i])) {
      et[i] = 0
      Kt = matrix(0, p, 1)
    } else {
      Kt = Rt[, , i] %*% t(Fi) / Qt[i]
      et[i] = y[i] - ft[i]
    }

    mt[i, ] = at[i, ] + drop(Kt * et[i])

    # Numerically stable covariance update
    A = diag(p) - Kt %*% Fi
    Ct[, , i] = A %*% Rt[, , i] %*% t(A) +
      V * Kt %*% t(Kt)

    ## predict next state
    at[i + 1, ] = GG %*% mt[i, ]
    Rt[, , i + 1] = GG %*% Ct[, , i] %*% t(GG) + W
  }

  colnames(mt) = c("a", "b")

  return(list(at = at, Rt = Rt, ft = ft, Qt = Qt,
              mt = mt, Ct = Ct, et = et))
}


In the Kalman filter function, Fi <- FF[i, , drop = FALSE] selects the observation matrix row \([1,z_i]\) for the current time point. The first entry multiplies the estimated intercept and the second multiplies the estimated slope. Therefore, ft[i] <- Fi %*% at[i, ] calculates predicted consumption growth as \(\hat{a}_{i|i-1}+z_i\hat{b}_{i|i-1}\)), using the coefficient estimates available before observing the current consumption value.


3. Estimate the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) by applying a Kalman filter and calculate \(\hat{x}_{T|T}\). You will need to write your own code to implement the Kalman filter. The only parameter that has not been specified is \(\sigma^2\). It makes no difference what value you use in your code. Why?


Show R code
# extracting values
y <- as.numeric(uschange[, "Consumption"])
z <- as.numeric(uschange[, "Income"])
N <- length(y)

# initializing and using the function
FF <- cbind(1, z)
GG <- diag(2)
W <- matrix(0, 2, 2)

V <- 1
m0 <- c(0, 0)
C0 <- V * 1e7 * diag(2)

fit <- Kfilter(
  FF = FF, GG = GG,
  m0 = m0, C0 = C0,
  W = W, V = V, y = y
)

# Final filtered coefficient estimates)
fit$mt[N, ]


        a         b 
0.5451038 0.2806012 


The first filtered estimate, fit$mt[1, ], updates the initial coefficient estimates using only the first observation. Each subsequent step incorporates another observation while retaining the information from earlier updates. Therefore, fit$mt[N, ] gives the final intercept and slope estimates using all (N) observations. The choice of (^2) does not affect these coefficient estimates because the common scale factor cancels in the Kalman gain. In the code, C0 is proportional to V and W is zero, so changing V scales both the predicted state covariance and the observation prediction variance by the same factor. Their ratio remains unchanged, giving the same coefficient updates. However, the estimated uncertainty still depends on (^2).


4. Check that your estimates are identical to the usual OLS estimates obtained with the lm function.


Show R code
comparison <-round(cbind(
  OLS = unname(coef(fit1)),
  Kalman = unname(fit$mt[N, ])
), 6)

rownames(comparison) <- c("Intercept", "Slope")
comparison |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3, caption="lm() coeffecients")



lm() coeffecients



OLS
Kalman




Intercept
0.545
0.545


Slope
0.281
0.281





The OLS and final Kalman filter estimates agree to three decimal places, with an intercept of 0.545 and a slope of 0.281. This confirms that, with constant coefficients and a diffuse initial prior, the Kalman filter reproduces the OLS estimates to the displayed precision.


5. Use your code to obtain the sequence of parameter estimates given by \(\hat{x}_{1|1}, \hat{x}_{2|2}, \ldots, \hat{x}_{T|T}\).


Show R code
parameter_estimates <- fit$mt
head(parameter_estimates)


                a          b
[1,]  0.316654946  0.3078713
[2,]  1.384651717 -0.7905971
[3,] -0.009212048  0.5361286
[4,] -0.108316241  0.6141210
[5,] -0.221027725  0.8626960
[6,] -0.226788540  0.8509087


The code parameter_estimates <- fit$mt stores the intercept and slope estimates after each observation. Early estimates may fluctuate more because they are based on limited information. As more observations are incorporated, uncertainty about the coefficients decreases and individual observations generally have less influence, so the estimates tend to stabilise.


6. Plot the parameters over time. Does it appear that a model with time-varying parameters would be better?


Show R code
# formatting to plot
parameter_data <- data.frame(
  time = as.numeric(time(uschange)),
  Intercept = fit$mt[, 1],
  Slope = fit$mt[, 2]
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -time,
    names_to = "parameter",
    values_to = "estimate"
  )

ols_values <- data.frame(
  parameter = c("Intercept", "Slope"),
  estimate = unname(coef(fit1))
)

# plots
ggplot(parameter_data, aes(time, estimate)) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_hline(
    data = ols_values,
    aes(yintercept = estimate),
    colour = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Coefficient estimate",
    title = "Filtered regression coefficient estimates"
  ) +
  theme_classic()









The intercept estimate fluctuates considerably at the beginning, then settles close to the full-sample OLS estimate. The slope takes longer to stabilise, showing periods of little change followed by further adjustments. Both estimates become more stable as additional observations are incorporated.
These plots alone do not provide strong evidence that time-varying coefficients are needed. The changes may reflect learning about constant coefficients as more data become available, particularly early in the sample. A comparison with a model allowing time-varying coefficients would help assess whether that additional flexibility improves the fit.


7. How would you estimate \(\sigma^2\) using your code?


Show R code
# Fitted values using the final intercept and slope
fitted_values <- drop(FF %*% fit$mt[N, ])

# Regression residuals
errors <- y - fitted_values

# Estimate observation error variance
sigma2_hat <- sum(errors^2) / (N - 2)
sigma2_hat


[1] 0.3631358




8. Repeat the above, but this time use the dlm package to implement the Kalman filter. Check that you get the same series of parameter estimates.


Show R code
# model construction
dlm_model <- dlmModReg(
  X = as.numeric(z),
  addInt = TRUE,
  dV = V,
  dW = c(0, 0),
  m0 = m0,
  C0 = C0
)

# dlm Kalman filter
dlm_fit <- dlmFilter(as.numeric(y), dlm_model)

# Removes the initial state row to align with fit$mt
dlm_estimates <- as.matrix(dlm_fit$m[-1, , drop = FALSE])
colnames(dlm_estimates) <- c("a", "b")

# comparison
comparison_h <- cbind(
  Own_filter = unname(fit$mt[N, ]),
  dlm = unname(dlm_estimates[N, ]),
  OLS = unname(coef(fit1))
)

rownames(comparison_h) <- c("Intercept", "Slope")
comparison_h |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3, caption = "Table comparing package to function")



Table comparing package to function



Own_filter
dlm
OLS




Intercept
0.545
0.545
0.545


Slope
0.281
0.281
0.281





Show R code
# Compare the complete sequence of estimates
max(abs(fit$mt - dlm_estimates))


[1] 8.226381e-10


The final coefficient estimates agree across the manually coded Kalman filter, the dlm package and OLS to the displayed precision. Comparing the complete sequence checks that the two Kalman filter implementations agree at every update, rather than only at the final observation. The maximum absolute difference between their sequences is very close to zero, indicating agreement within numerical precision.

Hidden Markov Models — Tutorial
text:
Question 1

1. Simulate 20 observations from the following three-state HMM. All three state distributions are two-dimensional Gaussian (Figure 5 in the notes):
\[
   [\mathbf{x}_t \mid z_t = k, \theta]
   \sim N(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \Sigma_k)
   \]
with transition probability matrix
\[
   \Gamma =
   \begin{pmatrix}
   0.8 & 0.1 & 0.1 \\
   0.1 & 0.8 & 0.1 \\
   0.1 & 0.1 & 0.8
   \end{pmatrix}.
   \]


Show R code
# mean vectors for the three states
mu <- 10 * matrix(
  c(-1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1),
  ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

# covariance matrices for the three states
sf <- 10
sigma <- array(0, dim = c(2, 2, 3))

sigma[, , 1] <- sf * matrix(c(1, 1/2, 1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma[, , 2] <- sf * matrix(c(1, -1/2, -1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma[, , 3] <- sf * matrix(c(3, 0, 0, 1/2), nrow = 2)

# transition probabilities between states
Gamma <- matrix(
  c(0.8, 0.1, 0.1,
    0.1, 0.8, 0.1,
    0.1, 0.1, 0.8),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE
)

# simulates the hidden states using a stationary initial distribution
set.seed(4010)
n <- 20
delta <- stationary(Gamma)
states <- simulate_states(n, Gamma, delta)

# each observation using its state's mean and covariance
observations <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = 2)

for (t in seq_len(n)) {
  k <- states[t]

  observations[t, ] <- mu[k, ] +
    drop(t(chol(sigma[, , k])) %*% rnorm(2))
}

# the observations and true states
simulated_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  x1 = observations[, 1],
  x2 = observations[, 2],
  state = factor(states, levels = 1:3)
)

simulated_data

20   20  10.0797588 -2.4425884     2


I first simulated 20 hidden states using the transition matrix and its stationary distribution, which assigns probability (1/3) to each initial state. The probability of remaining in the current state is 0.8, while the total probability of switching is 0.2, so runs within the same state are expected. Each observation was then generated from the bivariate Gaussian distribution associated with its state. The code selects the appropriate mean vector and covariance matrix using states[t]. Observations from the same state still differ because they are random draws from that distribution.


2. Plot the observations \(Y_t\), colour-coded by their true state. Also indicate the path of these observations, as this is a time series.


Show R code
# plots the observations 
ggplot(simulated_data, aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_path(
    aes(group = 1),
    colour = "grey60",
    arrow = grid::arrow(
      length = grid::unit(0.1, "inches")
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = state), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = time), nudge_y = 0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("1" = "blue", "2" = "red", "3" = "darkgreen"),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "First component",
    y = "Second component",
    colour = "True state"
  ) +
  theme_classic()









The plot shows three distinct groups corresponding to the hidden states. State 1 observations (blue) lie on the left, state 2 observations (red) on the lower right, and state 3 observations (green) towards the top. These locations are consistent with the specified mean vectors ((-10,0)), ((10,0)) and ((0,10)).
The numbered points and connecting lines show the sequence over time. Observations 1–7 remain in state 2, while observations 12–17 remain in state 3, illustrating the persistence encouraged by the 0.8 probability of staying in the current state. Other points show switches between states. Variation within each group reflects the randomness of the Gaussian observations and their state-specific covariance matrices.


3. If you had to estimate the parameters for this situation, given only the observations, what are the parameters, and how many are there?
If only the observations were available and all model parameters were unknown, I would estimate the transition probabilities and the mean vector and covariance matrix for each of the three states. Each transition matrix row has two free probabilities because its three entries must sum to one, giving \((3(3-1)=6\) free parameters. Each bivariate Gaussian distribution has two means and three distinct covariance parameters, giving \(3(2+3)=15\) parameters across the states. The total is therefore \(6+15=21\) free parameters when the initial distribution is determined by stationarity. If the initial distribution is estimated separately, it contributes two additional free parameters, giving 23. The hidden state sequence is inferred separately and is not included in this parameter count.

title: Hidden Markov Models — Tutorial
text:
Question 2
The following are 10 observations from a three-state HMM, with states A, B and C, and possible observations x, y and z:


Show R code
obs <- c("x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "z", "z", "y")


Use the following initial state probabilities, transition probability matrix and emission probability matrix:


Show R code
init <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)

tpm <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.6, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.2, 0.6),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

emmprob <- matrix(
  c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.5, 0.4,
    0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)



1. Use the Viterbi algorithm to find the most likely state sequence, given the observations.


Show R code
# observations and possible states
obs <- c(rep("x", 7), "z", "z", "y")
obsposs <- c("x", "y", "z")
state_names <- c("A", "B", "C")

# initial state probabilities
init <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)

# transition probabilities
tpm <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.6, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.2, 0.6),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

# emission probabilities
emmprob <- matrix(
  c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.5, 0.4,
    0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

# log probabilities 
log_init <- log2(init)
Gamma <- log2(tpm)
em.probs <- log2(emmprob)

n <- length(obs)
K <- length(state_names)

# best log score for each state at each time
xi <- matrix(0, nrow = K, ncol = n)

# initializes using the first observation
oi <- match(obs[1], obsposs)
xi[, 1] <- log_init + em.probs[, oi]

# calculates best path score ending in each state
for (i in 2:n) {
  oi <- match(obs[i], obsposs)

  for (j in seq_len(K)) {
    xi[j, i] <- max(xi[, i - 1] + Gamma[, j]) +
      em.probs[j, oi]
  }
}

# backtracks from the best final state
path <- integer(n)
path[n] <- which.max(xi[, n])

for (i in seq.int(n - 1, 1)) {
  path[i] <- which.max(xi[, i] + Gamma[, path[i + 1]])
}

# comparison
decoded <- state_names[path]
true_states <- c("A", "C", "A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B")

comparison <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  observation = obs,
  true_state = true_states,
  decoded_state = decoded
)

decoded


 [1] "A" "A" "A" "A" "A" "A" "A" "B" "B" "B"




2. Briefly explain and illustrate your results.


Show R code
# combine the true and decoded sequences for plotting
plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    time = seq_len(n),
    state = match(true_states, state_names),
    sequence = "True"
  ),
  data.frame(
    time = seq_len(n),
    state = path,
    sequence = "Viterbi"
  )
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(time, state, colour = sequence)) +
  geom_step() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(n)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = state_names) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("True" = "black", "Viterbi" = "blue")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "State", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









The Viterbi algorithm assigns state A to the first seven observations and state B to the final three. This is consistent with the emission probabilities, since A has the highest probability of producing x, while B can produce z and has the highest probability of producing y. The algorithm also accounts for transition probabilities when selecting the most likely complete sequence.
The decoded sequence agrees with the true sequence except at time 2, where it selects A instead of C. Although C can produce x, remaining in A gives a more probable overall path than switching to C and then returning to A. This illustrates that the most likely state sequence does not necessarily recover every true hidden state.

Question 3
Consider a stationary two-state Poisson HMM with parameters

\Gamma =

\end{pmatrix}
\]
and \(\lambda=(1,3)\).
In each of the following ways, compute the probability that the first three observations are \(0,2,1\).

1. Consider all possible sequences of states of the Markov chain that could have occurred. Compute the probability of each sequence and the probability of the observations given each sequence.


Show R code
# transition probabilities and state-specific Poisson means
Gamma3 <- matrix(
  c(0.1, 0.9,
    0.4, 0.6),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

x3 <- c(0, 2, 1)

delta3


[1] 0.3076923 0.6923077


Show R code
# paths
paths3 <- expand.grid(
  s1 = 1:2,
  s2 = 1:2,
  s3 = 1:2
)

# probability of each hidden state sequence
paths3$state_probability <- apply(paths3[, 1:3], 1, function(s) {
  delta3[s[1]] *
    Gamma3[s[1], s[2]] *
    Gamma3[s[2], s[3]]
})

# probabilities
paths3$observation_given_states <- apply(
  paths3[, 1:3], 1, function(s) {
    prod(dpois(x3, lambda = lambda3[s]))

  paths3$state_probability * paths3$observation_given_states

title: Hidden Markov Models — Tutorial
text:
Question 7: Two-state Bernoulli HMM
Assume a two-state Bernoulli HMM defined as follows.
The transition probability matrix is
\[
\Gamma =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5 & 0.5 \\
0.25 & 0.75
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The state-dependent distributions are given by
\[
P(X_t=x \mid C_t=1)=0.5,
\qquad x=0,1,
\]
and
\[
P(X_t=1 \mid C_t=2)=1.
\]
The stationary distribution is
\[
\delta=\frac{1}{3}(1,2).
\]
Find \(P(0)\) and \(P(1)\).
Write a function to calculate the likelihood.
Check that, for the observations \((X_1=1,X_2=1,X_3=1)\),
\[
L=\frac{29}{48}.
\]


Show R code
# transition probabilities
Gamma7 <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.5,
    0.25, 0.75),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

# stationary initial distribution
delta7 <- c(1/3, 2/3)

# probabilities
p7 <- c(0.5, 1)

# diagonal matrices of observation probabilities
P7 <- function(x) {
  diag(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = p7))
}

P7(0)


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  0.5    0
[2,]  0.0    0


Show R code
P7(1)


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  0.5    0
[2,]  0.0    1


Show R code
# Bernoulli HMM likelihood
bernoulli_likelihood <- function(x, log = FALSE) {
  stopifnot(length(x) > 0, all(x %in% c(0, 1)))

  phi = delta7
  ll = 0

  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    Pi = P7(x[i])

    if (i == 1) {
      v = phi %*% Pi
    } else {
      v = phi %*% Gamma7 %*% Pi
    }

    # normalizes and accumulate the log likelihood
    u = sum(v)

    if (u <= 0) {
      return(if (log) -Inf else 0)
    }

    ll <- ll + log(u)
    phi <- drop(v / u)
  }

  if (log) ll else exp(ll)
}


c(
  calculated = bernoulli_likelihood(c(1, 1, 1)),
  expected = 29/48
)

0.1 What changes at a structural break?
A structural break changes the relationship generating a series. A one-off outlier, a persistent level shift, a change in slope, a new variance and a changed seasonal pattern call for different models. An event date is a candidate explanation, not proof of a causal effect.

text:
0.2 Recognise the intervention shapes
At the first affected observation, a step becomes one. A ramp starts at zero and then increases: it changes slope while keeping the fitted curve continuous. Add both to allow a jump and a slope change.


Show R code
shapes <- data.frame(t = 1:120) |>
  mutate(Pulse = as.integer(t == 61),
         Step = as.integer(t >= 61),
         Ramp = pmax(0, t - 61),
         Temporary = as.integer(t >= 61 & t <= 85)) |>
  pivot_longer(-t, names_to = "type", values_to = "value")
ggplot(shapes, aes(t, value)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 61, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Intervention value")









Try: Move the break to observation 40. How does a pulse differ from a temporary shift lasting 25 observations?
Your answer:


Show R code
shapes <- data.frame(t = 1:120) |>
  mutate(Pulse = as.integer(t == 41),
         Step = as.integer(t >= 41),
         Ramp = pmax(0, t - 41),
         Temporary = as.integer(t >= 41 & t <= 65)) |>
  pivot_longer(-t, names_to = "type", values_to = "value")
ggplot(shapes, aes(t, value)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 41, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Intervention value")









The pulse is a short structural break where the intervention value increases at a single point in time and then immediately decreases back to its original level. This represents a one-off shock to the series.
A temporary break lasts for a longer period. The intervention value increases at observation 41 and stays constant at this new level until observation 65, after which it decreases back to its original level. Therefore, unlike a pulse, which only affects one observation, a temporary break affects the series for a specified period before returning to the original level.

0.3 A level shift: annual Nile flows
R’s documentation describes Nile as annual flow at Aswan, 1871–1970, with an apparent change point near 1898. First inspect the plot without imposing that date. Dataset documentation.

Show R code
# Search over one unknown break. b is the LAST observation of regime 1.
scan_level <- function(y, minimum = 15) {
  n <- length(y)
  stopifnot(n >= 2 * minimum, all(is.finite(y)))
  candidates <- minimum:(n - minimum)
  data.frame(last_before = candidates,
    RSS = vapply(candidates, function(b) {
      sum((y[1:b] - mean(y[1:b]))^2) +
        sum((y[(b + 1):n] - mean(y[(b + 1):n]))^2)
    }, numeric(1)))
}
scan_nile <- scan_level(nile$flow)
b_nile <- scan_nile$last_before[which.min(scan_nile$RSS)]
first_year <- nile$year[b_nile + 1]
first_year

The minimum segment length was changed to 10, 20 and 30 to determine whether changing the minimum number of observations allowed on either side of the structural break would affect the detected break point. The estimated break year remained the same across the different minimum segment lengths. This suggests that the detected structural break is relatively stable and is not sensitive to the choice of minimum segment length.
For each minimum segment length, a stable mean model and a level shift model were fitted. The stable mean model assumes that the mean of the Nile flow remains constant throughout the entire series, while the level shift model allows the mean to change after the detected structural break.
The ACF plots of the residuals were then compared. The stable mean model shows more autocorrelation in the residuals, while the level shift model shows a reduction in the autocorrelation after accounting for the structural break. This suggests that some of the autocorrelation that appears in the stable model may actually be caused by the unmodelled change in the mean rather than only by dependence between observations over time.
Therefore, not accounting for a structural break can make a series appear to have stronger persistence or autocorrelation than it actually has. Once the level shift is included in the model, some of this dependence is removed because the model is able to account for the different mean levels before and after the structural break.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
section: 0.4 A trend break without a level jump
text:
0.4 A trend break without a level jump
Here the true break is known, so you can assess whether your method recovers it. The generating mean is continuous at observation 121.


Show R code
set.seed(12)
trend_data <- data.frame(t = 1:240) |>
  mutate(after = as.integer(t >= 121), ramp = pmax(0, t - 121),
         true_mean = 10 + 0.04 * t + 0.12 * ramp,
         y = true_mean + rnorm(n(), sd = 1.3))
m_stable <- lm(y ~ t, data = trend_data)
m_level <- lm(y ~ t + after, data = trend_data)
m_slope <- lm(y ~ t + ramp, data = trend_data)
m_both <- lm(y ~ t + after + ramp, data = trend_data)
data.frame(model = c("Stable trend", "Level only", "Slope only", "Level and slope"),
           BIC = c(BIC(m_stable), BIC(m_level), BIC(m_slope), BIC(m_both)))

# Search for an unknown continuous slope break.
trend_scan <- data.frame(first_after = 37:204)
trend_scan$RSS <- vapply(trend_scan$first_after, function(k) {

Try: Add 5 * after to true_mean, regenerate y, and refit. Which model now has the smallest BIC? Interpret the pre-break slope and the change in slope separately.
Your answer:


Show R code
# set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(12)
# creates the data frame trend data where:
# after refers to the inccator variable where 0 is before and 1 is after 
# t = is the trend before the structural change/break
# ramp is the change is the trend, only kicks in after the strucutral break 
trend_data <- data.frame(t = 1:240) |> 
  mutate(
    after = as.integer(t >= 121),
    ramp = pmax(0,t-121),
    true_mean = 10 +0.04*t+5*after+0.12*ramp,
    y = true_mean + rnorm(n(), sd = 1.3)
  )


#regression for each model 
stable <- lm(y~t, data = trend_data)
level <- lm(y~t+after, data = trend_data)
slope <- lm(y~t + ramp , data = trend_data)
both <- lm(y~t + after+ramp , data = trend_data)

#datafram to represemt the performance (BIC) of each model 
data.frame(model = c("Stable trend new", "Level only new", "Slope only new", "Level and slope new"),
           BIC = c(BIC(stable), BIC(level), BIC(slope), BIC(both)))


                model       BIC
1    Stable trend new 1160.2668
2      Level only new 1111.1000
3      Slope only new  961.4940
4 Level and slope new  806.0392


The level and slope model now has the lowest BIC, while the stable trend model has the highest BIC. This is because the level and slope model aligns more closely with the DGP (data-generating process), since the data was generated with both a level change and a change in trend after the structural break.


Show R code
# slope model coefficients
coef(slope)


(Intercept)           t        ramp 
 8.55922519  0.07369154  0.11460591 


Show R code
# both model coeffecients
coef(both)


(Intercept)           t       after        ramp 
 9.78702233  0.04349981  4.79092067  0.11510495 


The output for the slope-only model shows the trend before observation 121 and the ramp, which represents the change in the trend after the structural break. The output for the level and slope model shows the trend before the break, the after coefficient, which represents the immediate change in level at the structural break, and the ramp, which represents the change in slope after the break.
The trend coefficient seems to decrease when the after component is added to the model, while the ramp coefficient stays relatively similar. This is because the slope-only model does not account for the immediate level change and therefore has to capture the structural change using only the trend and ramp terms. Adding the after variable allows the model to separately account for the immediate level change.
The post-break slope for the level and slope model is approximately 0.16. This is calculated by adding the pre-break trend coefficient and the ramp coefficient. Therefore, after the structural break, y increases by approximately 0.16 for every additional time period, assuming all other factors remain constant.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
section: 0.5 A variance break with no mean change
text:
0.5 A variance break with no mean change
A mean-break detector is not a variance-break detector. This example has known mean zero and independent Gaussian observations; those assumptions make the likelihood calculation especially simple.


Show R code
set.seed(25)
# rule is for observation <150 the standard deviation used is 1 and if greater than this then 3 is used
variance_data <- data.frame(t = 1:300) |>
  mutate(true_sd = ifelse(t <= 150, 1, 3),
         y = rnorm(n(), sd = true_sd), regime = ifelse(t <= 150, "Before", "After"))

# plot of this 
ggplot(variance_data, aes(t, y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 150.5, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Value")









Show R code
variance_data |> group_by(regime) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(y), variance = var(y), .groups = "drop")


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  regime   mean variance
  <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 After   0.128    9.82 
2 Before -0.153    0.882


Show R code
# Gaussian negative log likelihood, fixing the mean at its known value zero.
# The code below is trying to determine where the break is
variance_nll <- function(y) {
  v <- max(mean(y^2), 1e-12)
  -sum(dnorm(y, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(v), log = TRUE))
}
variance_scan <- data.frame(last_before = 30:270)
variance_scan$nll <- vapply(variance_scan$last_before, function(b) {
  variance_nll(variance_data$y[1:b]) +
    variance_nll(variance_data$y[(b + 1):300])
}, numeric(1))
variance_scan[which.min(variance_scan$nll), ]


    last_before      nll
122         151 587.6298


Show R code
# plot to show the likelihood
ggplot(variance_scan, aes(last_before + 1, nll)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Candidate first observation after break", y = "Negative log likelihood")









Try: Reverse the standard deviations, or use a gradual increase. In real data first remove a suitable mean model and inspect residuals and squared residuals. Contrast a single persistent variance shift with recurrent volatility clustering; they need not require the same model.
Your answer:
From the code provided, an increase in the standard deviation results in a larger spread of the observations around the mean. This creates a visible structural change in the variability of the series around observation 150.
To reverse the standard deviations, a standard deviation of 3 is assigned to observations before and including observation 150, while a standard deviation of 1 is assigned to observations after observation 150. This is shown in the code below


Show R code
variance_data_reverse <- data.frame(t = 1:300) |>
  mutate(true_sd = ifelse(t <= 150, 3, 1),
         y = rnorm(n(), sd = true_sd), regime = ifelse(t <= 150, "Before", "After"))


# plot of reversed
ggplot(variance_data_reverse, aes(t, y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 150.5, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Value")









Show R code
variance_data |> group_by(regime) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(y), variance = var(y), .groups = "drop")


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  regime   mean variance
  <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 After   0.128    9.82 
2 Before -0.153    0.882


The series now starts with a large spread of observations and, after the structural break, the spread becomes smaller. This is expected because the standard deviation decreases from 3 to 1.
To compare the mean and variance before and after the structural break, the following code is run:


Show R code
variance_data_reverse |>
  mutate(
    regime = ifelse(t <= 150, "Before", "After")
  ) |>
  group_by(regime) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(y),
    variance = var(y),
    sd = sd(y)
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3, caption = "Change in variance and mean before and after the structural break")



Change in variance and mean before and after the structural break


regime
mean
variance
sd




After
0.045
1.119
1.058


Before
0.012
7.280
2.698





The mean did change before the mean was smaller and after the structural break the mean became larger. This is makes sense as the observations after the break have less variability than the ones before the break. The variance also did change after the structural break which confirms that the code ran correctly.This confirms that the structural change in this example is primarily a change in variance rather than a change in mean.
The break search code will be run again to determine if the model is able to detect the break


Show R code
variance_nll <- function(y) {
  v <- max(mean(y^2), 1e-12)
  
  -sum(
    dnorm(y, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(v), log = TRUE)
  )
}

variance_scan <- data.frame(last_before = 30:270)

variance_scan$nll <- vapply(
  variance_scan$last_before,
  function(b) {
    
    variance_nll(variance_data_reverse$y[1:b]) +
      variance_nll(variance_data_reverse$y[(b + 1):300])
    
  },
  numeric(1)
)

variance_scan[which.min(variance_scan$nll), ]


    last_before      nll
122         151 581.9607


The function shows that the structural break is at observation 151, which is the same break point as before.
The structural break in the series in this example seems to come from the variance rather than the mean. Although the mean value changed slightly, the magnitude of the change was not very large in comparison to the change in the variance. The small change in the mean can be attributed to random variation, since the data before and after the break were generated with the same underlying mean.
Another thing to note is that the structural break only happens once, as the series moves from one variance regime to another. This is different from volatility clustering, where periods of high and low volatility occur repeatedly over time. If this type of recurring volatility were present in the data, then a volatility modelling approach, such as an ARCH or GARCH model, would be more appropriate for capturing the changing volatility over time.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
text:
0.6 A change in seasonal amplitude
Changing seasonality can be missed by a model that only includes a level step.


Show R code
set.seed(50)
#series where the seasonality appears every 12 months
seasonal_data <- data.frame(t = 1:240) |>
  mutate(after = as.integer(t >= 121),
         s = sin(2 * pi * t / 12), c = cos(2 * pi * t / 12),
         y = 20 + 0.02 * t + (2 + 4 * after) * s + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.8))

# regression models fitted 
season_stable <- lm(y ~ t + s + c, data = seasonal_data)
season_level <- lm(y ~ t + s + c + after, data = seasonal_data)
season_change <- lm(y ~ t + s + c + after + after:s + after:c,data = seasonal_data)

# data fram of output
data.frame(model = c("Stable season", "Level step", "Season interactions"),
           BIC = c(BIC(season_stable), BIC(season_level), BIC(season_change))) |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3, caption = "Table of BIC for the 3 models")



Table of BIC for the 3 models


model
BIC




Stable season
942.054


Level step
947.533


Season interactions
602.924





Show R code
# plot of the series and the break 
seasonal_data$fitted <- fitted(season_change)
ggplot(seasonal_data, aes(t, y)) + geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 121, linetype = 2) + labs(x = "Month", y = "Value")









Try: Replace the post-break wave by a phase-shifted wave. Fit month-factor interactions instead of a single sine/cosine pair. How many extra coefficients does each approach need?
Your answer:
From the code provided, the model with seasonal interactions has the lowest BIC, while the level-step model has the highest BIC of the three models.
To answer the question, the post-break seasonal wave will be shifted so that the seasonal peaks occur in different months rather than increasing in amplitude. Therefore, the magnitude of the seasonality will remain the same, but the timing of the peaks and troughs will change. I have decided to shift the seasonality by three months.


Show R code
# phase_shift model
seasonal_data_phase_shift <- data.frame(t = 1:240) |>
  mutate(after = as.integer(t >= 121),
         s = sin(2 * pi * t / 12),
         s_after = sin(2 * pi * (t - 3) / 12), # change was applied here
         y = 20 + 0.02 * t +ifelse(after == 0, 2 * s, 2 * s_after) +rnorm(n(), sd = 0.8)
  )


# plot of phase shift
ggplot(seasonal_data_phase_shift, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 121, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Observation",y = "y", title = "Plot showing phase shift")









The vertical line in the plot indicates the location of the structural break. The change in seasonality is less visually obvious than the previous change in amplitude because the magnitude of the seasonal fluctuations has not changed. Instead, the timing of the peaks and troughs has shifted by three months after the break. There is also an increasing linear trend in the series, which is generated by the 0.02 * t term.
To determine whether accounting for the structural break better captures the shifted seasonal pattern, month factors are created and two models are compared. The stable-seasonality model assumes that the effect of each month remains the same before and after the structural break. The changing-seasonality model allows the effect of each month to change after the structural break.


Show R code
seasonal_data_phase_shift <- seasonal_data_phase_shift |>
  mutate(
    month = factor((t - 1) %% 12 + 1)
  )

# regression models 
month_stable <- lm(y ~ t + month,data = seasonal_data_phase_shift)
month_change <- lm(y ~ t + month + after + month:after,data = seasonal_data_phase_shift)

# model comparison
data.frame(
  model = c("Stable month seasonality","Changing month seasonality"),
  BIC = c(BIC(month_stable),BIC(month_change))
) |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3, caption = "Table showing change BIC of stable seasonality vs shifted seasonality")



Table showing change BIC of stable seasonality vs shifted seasonality


model
BIC




Stable month seasonality
856.533


Changing month seasonality
726.702





The changing-seasonality model had a lower BIC. This means that when there is a shift in the seasonal pattern, detecting and accounting for the structural break allows the series to be fitted more accurately. If the seasonal pattern changes, 11 additional coefficients are required when using monthly factors, as an additional coefficient is needed for each month to capture changes in the monthly effects after the structural break. One month acts as a reference month and that is why only 11 additional coefficients are needed. A sine-cosine approach, however, only requires two additional coefficients to be estimated. Although this approach is more parsimonious, it may not capture complex changes in seasonality as accurately as the monthly-factor approach, which allows the effect of each month to change separately.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
text:
0.7 A real policy intervention: Seatbelts
The dataset records monthly drivers killed or seriously injured, not deaths alone. Compulsory seatbelt wearing began on 31 January 1983. Use the supplied law variable to encode exposure rather than guessing how the partial month was recorded. Dataset documentation.


Show R code
# data assigined
seat <- as.data.frame(Seatbelts)
seat$date <- seq(as.Date("1969-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = nrow(seat))
seat$t <- seq_len(nrow(seat)) / 12 # general trend over time 
seat$month <- factor(format(seat$date, "%m"), levels = sprintf("%02d", 1:12)) # for seasonality 
seat$log_drivers <- log(seat$drivers) # response var

# plot of series
ggplot(seat, aes(date, drivers)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("1983-02-01"), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Drivers killed or seriously injured")









Show R code
# ols model
seat_ols <- lm(log_drivers ~ t + month + log(kms) + PetrolPrice + law, data = seat)


# design matrix
X_seat <- model.matrix(~t + month + log(kms) + PetrolPrice + law, seat)[, -1]
seat_ar <- auto.arima(seat$log_drivers, xreg = X_seat,
                     stationary = TRUE, seasonal = FALSE,
                     allowdrift = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)

# data frame of arima coeffecients found 
data.frame(model = c("OLS", "Regression with ARMA errors"),
law_coefficient = c(coef(seat_ols)["law"], coef(seat_ar)["law"]),percentage_change = 100 * expm1(c(coef(seat_ols)["law"],coef(seat_ar)["law"]))) |> 
  knitr::kable(, digits = 3)





model
law_coefficient
percentage_change




OLS
-0.151
-14.002


Regression with ARMA errors
-0.161
-14.870





Show R code
checkresiduals(seat_ar, plot = FALSE) 



    Ljung-Box test

data:  Residuals from Regression with ARIMA(2,0,0) errors
Q* = 6.4923, df = 8, p-value = 0.5923

Model df: 2.   Total lags used: 10


The percentage calculation is conditional on the controls and model. A date dummy alone does not establish a causal effect. For a simple teaching model, month factors handle fixed seasonality and stationary ARMA errors handle remaining dependence; more elaborate seasonal error models can also be explored.
Try: Omit the controls, then omit the trend. Compare estimates and uncertainty. Use acf(residuals(seat_ols)) and acf(residuals(seat_ar)) to assess remaining dependence.
Your answer:
The first plot has a dotted line showing when the seatbelt law was introduced. The series contains a variable called law, which acts as an indicator variable to distinguish between the period before and after the seatbelt law was introduced.
To investigate the effect of including different explanatory variables, three models were fitted: a model containing only the law indicator, a model containing the control variables but no time trend, and the full model containing the time trend and all control variables.


Show R code
# only law model 
seat_no_controls <- lm(log_drivers ~ law, data = seat)

# control + law model
seat_no_trend <- lm(log_drivers ~ month + log(kms) + PetrolPrice + law,data = seat)

# full model 
seat_full <- lm(log_drivers ~ t + month + log(kms) + PetrolPrice + law,data = seat)

# table for comparison
data.frame(
  model = c("Law Model","Law + Control Model","Full Model"),
  law_coefficient = c(coef(seat_no_controls)["law"],coef(seat_no_trend)["law"],coef(seat_full)["law"]),
  percentage_change = 100 * expm1(c(coef(seat_no_controls)["law"],coef(seat_no_trend)["law"],coef(seat_full)["law"]))
) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Law coefficient and estimated percentage change in deaths"
  )



Law coefficient and estimated percentage change in deaths


model
law_coefficient
percentage_change




Law Model
-0.261
-22.980


Law + Control Model
-0.162
-14.944


Full Model
-0.151
-14.002





The magnitude of the law coefficient decreases as more explanatory variables are included in the model. Similarly, the estimated percentage change in deaths associated with the introduction of the law becomes smaller as additional variables are controlled for. This suggests that the law-only model may attribute some changes in deaths to the seatbelt law that can also be explained by other factors, such as seasonality, kilometres travelled, petrol prices, and the underlying time trend. However, the difference between the model containing the control variables without a trend and the full model containing the trend is relatively small. This suggests that adding the time trend has only a small additional effect on the estimated law coefficient once the other control variables have already been included.
The residual ACFs of the full OLS model and the regression model with ARMA errors are then compared:


Show R code
acf(
  residuals(seat_ols),
  main = "OLS residual ACF"
)









Show R code
acf(
  residuals(seat_ar),
  main = "ARMA regression residual ACF"
)









The ACF plot for the OLS model shows that there is still autocorrelation in the residuals, with lags 1 and 2 appearing to have significant autocorrelation. This indicates that the explanatory variables in the OLS model do not fully account for the time dependence in the series. In contrast, the residual ACF for the model with ARMA errors shows that most of this autocorrelation structure has been removed.
This highlights the importance for accounting for serial dependence in time series models because even though the other explanatory variables explained variation in deaths time was a factor as well. This was not accounted for in the OLS model but in the ARMA error model it was.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
section: 0.8 A transformation before declaring a break: AirPassengers
text:
0.8 A transformation before declaring a break: AirPassengers
AirPassengers contains monthly international airline passengers in thousands. Dataset documentation.


Show R code
# importing of airpassengers data 
air <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("1949-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 144),
                  passengers = as.numeric(AirPassengers)) |>
  mutate(log_passengers = log(passengers))

#ts plot
air |> pivot_longer(c(passengers, log_passengers)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) + geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Value")









Show R code
# strucural decomposition
air_stl <- stl(log(AirPassengers), s.window = "periodic")
air_components <- data.frame(date = air$date, as.data.frame(air_stl$time.series))
#plot 
air_components |> pivot_longer(-date) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) + geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs(x = "Month", y = NULL)









Does changing raw-scale seasonal amplitude necessarily imply a structural break? What does the log transformation change?
Your answer:
No, I do not think it does. I think this is because of the type of seasonality found in the series. The months in which the peaks occur remain the same; however, the amplitude is different and appears to increase over time based on the plot. This implies that the seasonality is multiplicative. This is confirmed when the series is log-transformed, as the seasonal fluctuations appear to have a more consistent amplitude throughout the series.
The STL plot further confirms this, as the seasonal component of the transformed series appears to follow the same seasonal cycles throughout the dataset, with a relatively consistent amplitude visually.

title: Structural breaks: an exploratory tutorial
section: 0.9 Japan visitor arrivals: prepare the data carefully
text:
0.9 Japan visitor arrivals: prepare the data carefully
This section develops your original Japan project. Keep the forecast target as visitor arrivals, rather than equating all arrivals with leisure tourists. See JNTO’s definitions. Country coverage and missing categories can change an aggregate; the audit below reports those features. The supplied export has some partially missing months in 1992, 2008 and 2012. For this exploratory exercise, sum the available country counts, preserve the missing-count flag, and call the result an available-country aggregate. This is not an assertion that the missing counts were zero. Check against JNTO’s published national total before using this as a national-demand model, and repeat the analysis on a reconciled series.


Show R code
raw <- read_csv("JNTO - Trends in Visitor Arrivals to Japan.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
required <- c("Year", "Month (abbr)", "Country/Area", "SUM(Visitor Arrivals)")
stopifnot(all(required %in% names(raw)))
raw <- raw |>
  mutate(month_number = match(sub("\\.$", "", `Month (abbr)`), month.abb),
         date = as.Date(sprintf("%04d-%02d-01", Year, month_number)),
         arrivals = as.numeric(`SUM(Visitor Arrivals)`))
stopifnot(!anyNA(raw$date), all(raw$arrivals >= 0 | is.na(raw$arrivals)))

# A total row plus its component countries would double-count arrivals.
total_rows <- raw |> filter(grepl("^(total|all countries|grand total)$",
                                  trimws(`Country/Area`), ignore.case = TRUE))
stopifnot(nrow(total_rows) == 0)
duplicates <- raw |> count(date, `Country/Area`) |> filter(n > 1)
stopifnot(nrow(duplicates) == 0)

monthly_audit <- raw |> group_by(date) |>
  summarise(countries = n_distinct(`Country/Area`),
            missing_counts = sum(is.na(arrivals)),
            all_missing = all(is.na(arrivals)),
            visitors = if (all_missing) NA_real_ else sum(arrivals, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(date)

0.9.1 Explore levels, seasons and possible regimes
Use March 2020 as an illustrative disruption-window start; it is a modelling choice, not a claim that all restrictions started simultaneously. The reopening marker is October 2022, when independent travel and visa exemptions resumed. JNTO announcement.


Show R code
#ts plot of 2020-2022
ggplot(japan, aes(date, visitors)) + geom_line(colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2022-10-01")), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Available-country visitor arrivals", title = "Monthly arrivals in the supplied export")









Show R code
# Only compare complete years and complete quarters.
annual <- japan |> mutate(year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))) |>
  group_by(year) |> summarise(months = n(), visitors = sum(visitors), .groups = "drop")
annual |> filter(months == 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, visitors)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Complete year", y = "Annual visitor arrivals")









Show R code
quarterly <- japan |>
  mutate(quarter = tsibble::yearquarter(date)) |>
  group_by(quarter) |> summarise(months = n(), visitors = sum(visitors), .groups = "drop")
quarterly |> filter(months == 3) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(quarter), visitors)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Complete quarter", y = "Quarterly visitor arrivals")









Show R code
#plot showing before and after the distruption
japan <- japan |> mutate(regime = case_when(
  date < as.Date("2020-03-01") ~ "Before disruption",
  date < as.Date("2022-10-01") ~ "Disruption window",
  TRUE ~ "After reopening"))
ggplot(japan, aes(month, log_visitors, colour = regime)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Calendar month", y = "log(1 + arrivals)", colour = "Period")









Identify candidate level, slope and seasonal changes. Explain why a lower annual total in a partial year would be misleading. Are the seasonal boxplots confounded by long-run growth?
Your answer:
From the plots, it looks like there is a temporary structural break in the data. The series did not simply change permanently to a different level, as tourism collapsed during COVID-19 and then recovered after reopening. It is also not a pulse because the disruption lasted for a long period rather than a single observation.
The main candidate break is around 2020, where there is a drastic decline in tourist arrivals. After reopening, there is another change as arrivals increase rapidly, suggesting a change in both the level and slope of the series.
The boxplots also suggest that the seasonal pattern may have changed across the three periods. During the disruption, there is generally greater variation, while after reopening the level of arrivals is much higher. The timing and size of some seasonal peaks also appear different. However, these differences may also be affected by the different overall levels and trends across the three periods.


0.9.2 Build intervention variables and reserve a test set
Keep the last 12 months out of estimation. The break dates below are pre-specified event-based choices, not dates chosen using the test-set outcomes. A window captures temporary disruption; the reopening step and ramp allow a different subsequent level and growth rate. These are deliberately simple teaching models: one log-linear trend across several decades may be inadequate.


Show R code
add_interventions <- function(d) {
  month_id <- as.integer(format(d$date, "%Y")) * 12 +
    as.integer(format(d$date, "%m"))
  d |> mutate(
    disruption = as.integer(date >= as.Date("2020-03-01") & date < as.Date("2022-10-01")),
    reopened = as.integer(date >= as.Date("2022-10-01")),
    recovery_ramp = pmax(0, month_id - (2022 * 12 + 10)) / 12)
}
japan <- add_interventions(japan)
h <- 12
n_train <- nrow(japan) - h
train <- japan[seq_len(n_train), ]
test <- japan[(n_train + 1):nrow(japan), ]
range(train$date)


[1] "1990-01-01" "2025-05-01"


Show R code
range(test$date)


[1] "2025-06-01" "2026-05-01"


Show R code
X_base <- function(d) model.matrix(~t + month, d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
X_break <- function(d) model.matrix(~t + month + disruption + reopened + recovery_ramp,
                                    d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
fit_regression <- function(d, design) {
  auto.arima(d$log_visitors, xreg = design(d), stationary = TRUE,
             seasonal = FALSE, allowdrift = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
}
baseline <- fit_regression(train, X_base)
intervention <- fit_regression(train, X_break)
recent_train <- train |> filter(date >= as.Date("2022-10-01"))
stopifnot(nrow(recent_train) >= 24)
recent <- fit_regression(recent_train, X_base)


Month factors capture a fixed seasonal shape; ARMA errors handle remaining dependence. Reopening seasonality could instead be allowed to interact with month, but the short recent sample makes that a costly model. All fits above use log(1 + visitors) so zeros are allowed.


0.9.3 Compare out-of-sample forecasts


Show R code
prediction_frame <- function(model, future, design, label) {
  p <- forecast(model, xreg = design(future), level = 95)
  data.frame(date = future$date, model = label,
             prediction = pmax(0, expm1(as.numeric(p$mean))),
             lower = pmax(0, expm1(p$lower[, 1])),
             upper = pmax(0, expm1(p$upper[, 1])))
}
predictions <- bind_rows(
  prediction_frame(baseline, test, X_base, "Stable regression"),
  prediction_frame(intervention, test, X_break, "Intervention regression"),
  prediction_frame(recent, test, X_base, "Recent regime"),
  data.frame(date = test$date, model = "Seasonal naive",
    prediction = tail(train$visitors, 12), lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_)) |>
  left_join(select(test, date, observed = visitors), by = "date")
scores <- predictions |> group_by(model) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((observed - prediction)^2)),
            MAE = mean(abs(observed - prediction)),
            coverage95 = if (all(is.na(lower))) NA_real_ else mean(observed >= lower & observed <= upper),
            .groups = "drop") |> arrange(RMSE)
scores

3 Stable regression       1103744.  931639.          1

Show R code
# View point forecasts separately so wide intervals do not hide their differences.
ggplot(predictions, aes(date, prediction)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed), colour = "black") + facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(x = "Held-out month", y = "Visitor arrivals",
       subtitle = "Point forecasts: black observed, blue predicted median")









Show R code
ggplot(predictions, aes(date, prediction)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.15, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed), colour = "black") + facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(x = "Held-out month", y = "Visitor arrivals",
       subtitle = "Black: observed; blue: prediction and conditional 95% limits")









The back-transformed predictions are medians under Gaussian log-scale forecasts, not bias-adjusted arithmetic means. RMSE and MAE are therefore comparisons of these particular point forecasts. Interval limits condition on the specified interventions and model; they exclude uncertainty about future breaks. Twelve observations provide a noisy estimate of coverage. Do not compare information criteria across the full-history and recent-only fits: their estimation samples differ.
Which model performs best? Does the recent-only fit lose useful information or avoid an obsolete relationship? Which model would you choose for practical forecasting, and why?
Your answer:
The seasonal naïve model performed the best, while the recent-regime model had the second-lowest forecast error. The recent-regime forecast slightly overpredicts the actual values, but the pattern of the series appears to have changed after COVID-19. This suggests that some of the older data may no longer be as relevant for forecasting the current tourism regime.
The intervention model performed the worst, showing that keeping the full history and accounting for the structural changes did not improve forecast performance in this case. The intervention model also had a large prediction interval, and its forecasts increasingly deviated from the actual values.
For practical forecasting, I would choose the recent-regime model despite the seasonal naïve model having the lowest forecast error. The recent-regime model still performed well and focuses on the newer tourism regime, which appears to be more representative of the current behaviour of the series. This supports the idea that fitting the model using the more recent regime can be more useful for forecasting when past relationships have become less relevant.


0.9.4 Diagnose and forecast under an explicit scenario


Show R code
resid_japan <- as.numeric(na.omit(residuals(intervention)))
acf_japan <- acf(resid_japan, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 36)
data.frame(lag = as.numeric(acf_japan$lag)[-1], acf = as.numeric(acf_japan$acf)[-1]) |>
  ggplot(aes(lag, acf)) + geom_col(width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(length(resid_japan)), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Lag in months", y = "Residual ACF")









Show R code
# Demonstrate the intervention model; this is not automatic winner selection.
final_model <- fit_regression(japan, X_break)
future_dates <- seq(max(japan$date), by = "month", length.out = 13)[-1]
future <- data.frame(date = future_dates,
  t = max(japan$t) + (1:12) / 12,
  month = factor(format(future_dates, "%m"), levels = levels(japan$month))) |>
  add_interventions()
future_forecast <- prediction_frame(final_model, future, X_break, "No new break scenario")

What assumptions do the future intervention columns encode? How would the forecast change if recovery growth flattened? What would happen if a new restriction occurred?
Your answer:
Different future scenarios would need to be encoded depending on whether the disruption ends, the reopened regime continues, and whether the recovery ramp continues or flattens.
The residual ACF shows that there is still significant autocorrelation, suggesting that the model has not captured all of the time dependence in the series. If recovery flattened, the upward trend in the forecast would also flatten.
If a new disruption occurred while the model still assumed that reopening and recovery continued, it could incorrectly forecast increasing arrivals. Therefore, a new structural change would require the intervention variables to be updated to represent the new regime and the recovery ramp to be stopped or adjusted.

title: ARCH and GARCH Theory
text:
Investigate how ARCH and GARCH models describe volatility clustering, distinguish conditional from unconditional variance, and connect dependence in squared innovations to volatility forecasting and model diagnostics.



Write the observed process as
\[
y_t=\mu_t+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t=\sigma_t z_t,
\]
where \(\mu_t=E(y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})\), \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) denotes information available through time \(t-1\), and \(z_t\) are independent and identically distributed with mean zero and variance one, independent of \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\). The positive quantity \(\sigma_t\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\). Set \(h_t=\sigma_t^2\).
Follow the course notes’ convention:
\[
\text{ARCH}(q):\quad h_t=\alpha_0+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_i\varepsilon_{t-i}^2,
\]
\[
\text{GARCH}(p,q):\quad h_t=\alpha_0+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_i\varepsilon_{t-i}^2
+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j h_{t-j}.
\]
Assume \(\alpha_0>0\), \(\alpha_i\geq0\) and \(\beta_j\geq0\). Use a causal stationary solution wherever stationarity is specified. State additional moment assumptions when needed. A white-noise sequence has constant finite variance and zero autocovariances at nonzero lags; independence is a stronger property.



Let \(P_t>0\) be an asset price. Define its simple return and log return by
\[
R_t=\frac{P_t-P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}},\qquad
r_t=\log P_t-\log P_{t-1}.
\]
(a) [3] Show that \(r_t=\log(1+R_t)\), and prove that \[
\lim_{R_t\to0}\frac{r_t}{R_t}=1.
\]
(b) [2] Show that log returns add over time. Explain one reason to model returns rather than price levels.
(c) [3] A return series has negligible sample autocorrelation, but its squared returns have positive autocorrelation across many lags. Explain why these findings are compatible and what they suggest about the conditional mean and conditional variance.
(d) [2] Explain how constant-width prediction intervals can misrepresent uncertainty during calm and turbulent periods.
Your response:




Solution 1A





Solution 1B



The reason returns instead of prices are modelled is because prices tend to follow a random work in financial data. This makes them very difficult to model. The variance of prices is also unbounded meaning the spread can be very large.



This is compatible because the returns themselves having no autocorrelation is based on the efficiency market hypothesis that is the returns had a strong linear autocorrelation that traders would exploit this relationship by buying stocks at a lower price than they sell until there is no longer a linear autocorrelation between returns. However the presence of no linear autocorrelation does no imply there is no autocorrelation. it therefore makes sense that the squared returns have a positive correlation amongst many lags. I think it also links to the fact that there is volatility clustering seen when you plot the returns.



constant width prediction intervals are a problem because the conditional variance is heteroskedastic. Constant width prediction intervals implies the the conditional variance in heteroskedastic. For financial data this is a problem because this means that the risk could possibly be understated and overstated. This would thus impact the decisions that an individual makes. Therefore a prediction interval where the conditional variance is homoskedastic would not work.



Consider \[
\varepsilon_t=\sqrt{h_t}z_t,\qquad
h_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\varepsilon_{t-1}^2,
\qquad 0<\alpha_1<1.
\] Assume a causal stationary solution with finite second moment exists.
(a) [4] Derive \(E(\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})\). Justify the use of independence in each derivation.
(b) [4] Derive the unconditional mean and variance of \(\varepsilon_t\), stating where stationarity is used.
(c) [4] Prove that \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_t,\varepsilon_{t-k})=0\) for every integer \(k\geq1\). Explain why this does not establish independence.
(d) [3] Explain the parameter restrictions and how the model generates volatility clustering despite the result in part (c).
Your response:




Solution 2A





Solution 2B


The covariance only measures linear dependence and so this does not mean that there is non linear independence. 
the parameter restriction is due to the unconditional variance as found in question a). \(\\alpha_0 = 1\) then it would be undefined.




A fitted conditional mean model produces residuals with the following features:

Their ACF is close to zero at all nonzero lags.
Their squared values have positive autocorrelation that declines slowly.
Large positive and negative residuals occur in clusters.
A normal quantile plot shows more extreme observations in both tails than a normal distribution would suggest.

(a) [4] A student concludes: “The residuals are white noise, so there is nothing left to model.” Assess this statement. Distinguish what the residual ACF tells you from what it cannot tell you.
(b) [3] Explain what volatility clustering means in this example. Does a large negative residual imply that the next residual will probably also be negative? Justify your answer.
(c) [4] Another student proposes adding many AR terms to the conditional mean equation to remove the correlation in squared residuals. Explain whether this addresses the observed problem. What type of model would you investigate instead, and why?
(d) [4] Suppose an ARCH model assumes Gaussian standardized innovations. A reviewer argues that this contradicts the heavy tails in the residuals. Assess the argument by distinguishing the standardized innovations, the conditional distribution of residuals and their unconditional distribution. No moment derivation is required.
Your response:
a) The acf of residuals tells you if there is is linear autocorrelation present in the data. It cannot tell you if there is non linear autocorrelation nor can it tell you which model is the correct model. You can also use it to determine how many lag are significantly correlated with each other, however it can be very difficutl to conclude the correct model by just visually looking.
b) It means that large residuals are followed by large residuals and small residuals are followed by small residuals. This means the extent of the volatility appear in same groups of time as thought with the same extent. Yes a large residual implies the next residual will be large as the effect of volatility is relatively persistent and the effect takes a long time to damper off on future time periods.
c) The problem is that the result to be estimating a lot of parameters, this results in the likelihood surface being flat and makes it difficult to find reasonable estimates for the all the parameter values. Instead it is better to use a GARCH model instead as you can then model the past innovations in such a way that a lot of parameters do not need to be added to the model.
d) The reviewer’s argument is not entirely correct, because it confuses three different objects. The standardized innovations z_t are i.i.d. with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and under the model they are Gaussian with constant variance. The residuals are a function of these innovations, ε_t = σ_t z_t, so conditional on the past (when σ_t is known) they are also normal, N(0, σ_t²), but with a variance that changes over time. Unconditionally, the residuals are therefore a scale mixture of normals, since each observation is drawn from a normal with a different standard deviation, and this mixture has heavier tails than a single normal with the same overall variance.



Two GARCH(1,1) models have been proposed for daily returns measured in percentage points:



Model
\(\alpha_0\)
\(\alpha_1\)
\(\beta_1\)




A
0.02
0.05
0.90


B
0.02
0.25
0.70



Both use \[
h_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\varepsilon_{t-1}^2+\beta_1h_{t-1}.
\]
You may use \[
s=\alpha_1+\beta_1,\qquad \bar h=\frac{\alpha_0}{1-s}.
\]
(a) [3] Calculate each model’s persistence and long-run variance. What do these quantities tell you about similarities between the models?

\[

\]

the squared standardized residuals should show no remaining autocorrelation, which can be checked with ACF plots and a Ljung-Box test
the standardized residuals should pass an ARCH LM test, meaning we fail to reject the null of no remaining ARCH effects
