title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Daily Log Returns
The daily log return series is plotted below to examine how the magnitude of returns changes over time.


Click to expand code
# Converting to a tsibble so I can use the tidyverse for plotting
tktbl <- tk_tbl(log_ret, preserve_index = TRUE, rename_index = "Date")
JTOPI_ret <- as_tsibble(tktbl)

JTOPI_ret |> 
  autoplot(J200.JO.Adjusted) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Log Returns of the JSE Top 40 Index (2017-2026)",
    y = "Log Return",
    x = "Date"
  )









The plot shows alternating periods of relatively small and large return movements. Large movements tend to occur close together, while quieter periods also cluster together. This pattern is known as volatility clustering and is a common characteristic of financial return series.
The most pronounced fluctuations appear in 2020, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated disruption to financial markets. Further periods of elevated volatility are visible at the beginning of 2021 and during 2022, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine increased geopolitical and economic uncertainty.
Elevated volatility is also visible during parts of 2025 and early 2026. Potential contributing factors include developments in commodity and precious metals markets, as well as US and Israeli attacks on Iran and the associated uncertainty surrounding oil prices and commodity markets. These explanations provide context for the observed movements, although the return plot alone cannot establish a causal relationship between particular events and changes in volatility.
In contrast, the period before 2018 and parts of late 2024 appear comparatively calm. Overall, the concentration of large and small return movements into distinct periods suggests that return variability changes over time, motivating further investigation of conditional variance models.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Stylised Facts of Financial Returns
Four characteristics commonly examined when assessing financial return series are:

Weak autocorrelation in returns.
Persistent autocorrelation in squared returns.
Volatility clustering.
Heavy-tailed return distributions.

Volatility clustering was evident in the daily return plot. The remaining characteristics are examined below.

Autocorrelation in Returns and Squared Returns
The autocorrelation function (ACF) is used to examine linear dependence in returns. The ACF of squared returns provides an indication of whether the magnitude of returns exhibits persistent dependence.


Click to expand code
r <- JTOPI_ret$J200.JO.Adjusted

# plotting using patchwork
p_acf <- ggAcf(r, lag.max = 40) + 
  ggtitle("ACF of Log Returns") +
  theme_minimal()

p_acf_sq <- ggAcf(r^2, lag.max = 40) + 
  ggtitle("ACF of Squared Log Returns") +
  theme_minimal()

p_acf | p_acf_sq









The ACF of log returns contains some significant spikes, but these do not form a clear, persistent pattern across the displayed lags. This suggests that linear dependence in returns is relatively limited, although the significant spikes warrant consideration when specifying the mean equation.
In contrast, the ACF of squared returns shows more persistent autocorrelation, with a gradual decline across lags. This indicates that the magnitude of a return is related to the magnitude of previous returns, even when the direction of returns is difficult to predict. This pattern is consistent with volatility clustering and supports investigating a time-varying conditional variance model.


Distribution of Returns
A normal quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plot is used to compare the empirical distribution of daily returns with a normal distribution.


Click to expand code
r_vals <- as.data.frame(r)

#plot to check for nromality
ggplot(r_vals, aes(sample = r)) +
  stat_qq() + 
  stat_qq_line(color = "red", linewidth = 1) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Q-Q Plot of JSE Top 40 Daily Returns",
    x = "Theoretical Normal Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  )









The observations deviate from the reference line in the tails, indicating that extreme returns occur more frequently than would be expected under a normal distribution. This provides visual evidence of heavy tails.
Kurtosis provides an additional descriptive measure of tail behaviour. The calculation below uses Pearson kurtosis, for which a normal distribution has a value of 3.


Click to expand code
pearson_kurtosis <- kurtosis(r)


The Pearson kurtosis is 6.616. A value greater than 3 is consistent with heavier tails than those of a normal distribution.
Heavy tails describe the unconditional distribution of returns; they do not, by themselves, establish that conditional variance changes over time. Evidence of time-varying conditional variance is assessed more directly using the tests below.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
section: Formal Tests for ARCH Effects and Serial Dependence
text:
Formal Tests for ARCH Effects and Serial Dependence

Engle’s ARCH-LM Test
Engle’s ARCH-LM test is used to assess whether squared innovations exhibit dependence on their past values. For this preliminary test, returns are centred by subtracting their sample mean, consistent with the proposed constant mean specification.
Using 12 lags, the hypotheses are:

\(H_0\): There are no ARCH effects up to lag 12.
\(H_1\): ARCH effects are present at one or more of these lags.



Click to expand code
arch_test <- FinTS::ArchTest(r, lags = 12, demean = TRUE)
arch_test



    ARCH LM-test; Null hypothesis: no ARCH effects

data:  r
Chi-squared = 557.88, df = 12, p-value < 2.2e-16


The p-value is <0.001. A p-value below 0.05 leads to rejection of the null hypothesis at the 5% significance level and provides evidence of ARCH effects.
Such a result supports modelling conditional variance using an ARCH or GARCH specification, although it does not identify which particular model is most suitable.


Ljung–Box Test on Squared Returns
The Ljung–Box test is applied to squared returns to assess whether they exhibit serial correlation across the first 10 lags. It is a joint test across these lags, rather than a test of lag 10 alone.
The hypotheses are:

\(H_0\): Squared returns have zero autocorrelation at lags 1 through 10.
\(H_1\): Squared returns have non-zero autocorrelation at one or more of these lags.



Click to expand code
r2 <- r^2

lb_squared <- Box.test(r2, type = "Ljung-Box", lag = 10)
lb_squared



    Box-Ljung test

data:  r2
X-squared = 1445.3, df = 10, p-value < 2.2e-16


The p-value is <0.001. A p-value below 0.01 leads to rejection of the null hypothesis at the 1% significance level, providing evidence of serial dependence in squared returns.
Together with volatility clustering and the ARCH-LM test, significant dependence in squared returns supports the use of a time-varying conditional variance model.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Implications for Model Selection
The exploratory analysis identifies volatility clustering, persistent dependence in squared returns, and a heavy-tailed return distribution. These features motivate the comparison of GARCH models and the consideration of a heavy-tailed innovation distribution.
The formal tests assess whether the evidence against a constant conditional variance is statistically significant. Model comparison and residual diagnostics are then needed to determine which GARCH specification adequately captures the observed dependence.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
GARCH(1,1) Model from First Principles
The generalised autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model describes conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations and past conditional variances. Under suitable conditions, it can be represented as an ARCH model with infinitely many lags, providing a parsimonious way to capture the persistent effects of past shocks.
The GARCH(1,1) model with a constant mean is specified as
\[
r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad
\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t,
\]
\[
\sigma_t^2
=
\omega
+
\alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2
+
\beta \sigma_{t-1}^2,
\]
where:

\(\mu\) is the conditional mean return.
\(\omega\) is the variance intercept.
\(\alpha\) measures the immediate response of volatility to a shock.
\(\beta\) measures the persistence of past conditional variance.
\(z_t\) is a standardized innovation with mean zero and variance one.

The conditions \(\omega \> 0\), \(\alpha \geq 0\), and \(\beta \geq 0\) ensure positive conditional variances. The additional condition \(\alpha + \beta \< 1\) implies a finite unconditional variance under the standard model assumptions.

Recursive Variance Calculation
The model is implemented from first principles using a recursive loop. The initial conditional variance is set equal to the sample variance of returns. Each subsequent conditional variance is calculated using the previous squared innovation and conditional variance.
Returns are multiplied by 100 before estimation to improve numerical scaling. The resulting series therefore expresses log returns in percentage units.


Click to expand code
ret_perc <- as.numeric(r) * 100 # scaled because optim struggles with small values 

# function for garch implementation once optimal values are found
garch_func <- function(par, ret) {
  mu    = par[1]
  omega = par[2]
  alpha = par[3]
  beta  = par[4]
  eps   = ret - mu
  sig1  = numeric(length(ret))
  sig1[1] <- var(ret)
  # loop for garch model translating an arch model that is somewhat infinite
  for (i in 2:length(ret)) {
    sig1[i] =  omega + alpha * eps[i - 1]^2 + beta * sig1[i - 1]
  }
  list(eps = eps, sig1 = sig1)
}




Likelihood and Parameter Estimation
For the first-principles implementation, the standardised innovations are assumed to follow a normal distribution. Conditional on the initial variance, the Gaussian negative log-likelihood is
\[
-\ell(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\left[
\ln(2\pi)
+
\ln(\sigma_t^2)
+
\frac{\varepsilon_t^2}{\sigma_t^2}
\right],
\]
where \(\theta = (\mu,\omega,\alpha,\beta)\).
The optimiser searches for the parameter values that minimise this expression, which is equivalent to maximising the likelihood. Parameter combinations that violate the variance constraints are assigned a large penalty.


Click to expand code
garch_loglik <- function(par, ret) {
  omega = par[2]
  alpha = par[3]
  beta  = par[4]
  if (omega <= 0 || alpha < 0 || beta < 0 || alpha + beta >= 0.9999) {
    return(1e10)
  }
  f = garch_func(par, ret)
  0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi) + log(f$sig1) + f$eps^2 / f$sig1)
}

#initial starting values 
initial <- c(mu = mean(ret_perc), omega = 0.05 * var(ret_perc), alpha = 0.10, beta = 0.85)

# garch parameter estimated obtained for GARCH(1,1) 
g11 <- optim(initial, fn = garch_loglik, ret = ret_perc,
             method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(-1, 1e-6, 1e-6, 1e-6),
             upper = c( 1, 10,   0.999, 0.999),
             hessian = TRUE)

#check for convergence
g11$convergence # showed convergence


[1] 0


Click to expand code
# coefficients and standard errors for estimated parameters
errors <- sqrt(diag(solve(g11$hessian)))

round(cbind(Estimate = g11$par,SE = errors,z = g11$par / errors),4)


      Estimate     SE       z
mu      0.0582 0.0208  2.7952
omega   0.0412 0.0136  3.0287
alpha   0.0841 0.0147  5.7192
beta    0.8883 0.0215 41.3510


The optimizer returned a convergence code of zero, indicating successful numerical termination. The estimated standard errors were relatively small, although these are approximate Hessian-based standard errors under the Gaussian likelihood specification. Numerical convergence alone does not establish that the model is correctly specified or that the global optimum has been found.


Volatility Persistence
For a standard GARCH(1,1) model, volatility persistence is measured by \(\alpha + \beta\). Values close to one indicate that the effects of shocks decay slowly.


Click to expand code
# Calculate volatility persistence
persistence <- unname(g11$par[3] + g11$par[4])
persistence


[1] 0.9723304


Click to expand code
# Calculate the implied unconditional variance
long_run_variance <- unname(
  g11$par[2] / (1 - persistence)
)

long_run_variance


[1] 1.490001


The estimated persistence is 0.97233, indicating that volatility shocks are persistent. Since this value is below one, the model implies a finite unconditional variance:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(r_t)
=
\frac{\omega}{1-\alpha-\beta}.
\]
Because returns were scaled by 100, this variance is expressed in squared percentage units.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Comparison with the rugarch Package
The first-principles estimates are compared with a standard GARCH(1,1) model fitted using rugarch. The package model uses a constant mean and standardised Student’s t innovations to accommodate the heavy tails identified in the exploratory analysis.


Click to expand code
# Standard GARCH (sGARCH)
spec_g11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_g11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_g11, data = ret_perc, solver = "hybrid")
round(coef(fit_g11), 4)


    mu  omega alpha1  beta1  shape 
0.0641 0.0386 0.0762 0.8968 6.2416 


In the reported results, the rugarch model has a larger variance intercept and a larger coefficient on past conditional variance, but a smaller coefficient on the previous squared innovation than the first-principles model. This suggests a weaker immediate response to shocks and a greater contribution from past conditional variance.
However, the two implementations use different innovation distributions. The first-principles model uses a Gaussian likelihood, whereas the package model uses a Student’s t likelihood. Their estimates therefore need not coincide. Differences in variance initialization, optimization methods, and parameter constraints may also contribute.
A direct implementation check would require both models to use the same innovation distribution and comparable estimation settings.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Alternative GARCH Specifications
Four additional GARCH specifications are fitted to examine whether they capture features that the standard model does not. All package models use a constant mean and standardized Student’s t innovations.

Integrated GARCH
The integrated GARCH (iGARCH) model imposes
\[
\alpha + \beta = 1.
\]
Its persistence is therefore exactly one, rather than simply close to one. Under the usual specification with a positive intercept, the model does not have a finite unconditional variance, and volatility shocks do not decay in the same way as in a stationary standard GARCH model.


Click to expand code
## Other garch models
# Integrated GARCH (iGARCH)
spec_ig11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "iGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_ig11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_ig11, data = ret_perc, solver = "hybrid")




GJR-GARCH
The GJR-GARCH model allows positive and negative innovations to have different effects on subsequent volatility:
\[
\sigma_t^2
=
\omega
+
\left[
\alpha + \gamma I(\varepsilon_{t-1}<0)
\right]\varepsilon_{t-1}^2
+
\beta \sigma_{t-1}^2.
\]
The indicator equals one when the previous innovation is negative and zero otherwise. Positive innovations therefore have a coefficient of \(\alpha\), while negative innovations have a coefficient of \(\alpha+\gamma\). If \(\gamma\>0\), negative innovations increase conditional variance more than positive innovations of the same magnitude.


Click to expand code
# GJR-GARCH 
spec_gjrg11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_gjrg11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_gjrg11, data = ret_perc, solver = "hybrid")




Exponential GARCH
The exponential GARCH (eGARCH) model describes the logarithm of conditional variance. Exponentiating the fitted log variance ensures that conditional variance is positive, so the same non-negativity constraints used in the standard GARCH model are not required. The model also allows asymmetric responses to innovations.


Click to expand code
# Exponential GARCH (eGARCH)
spec_eg11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "eGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_eg11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_eg11, data = ret_perc, solver = "hybrid")




Component GARCH
The component GARCH model separates conditional variance into a time-varying long-run component and a transitory component. This allows short-run volatility movements to be distinguished from more persistent changes in the underlying volatility level.


Click to expand code
# Component GARCH (csGARCH)
spec_csg11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "csGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_csg11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_csg11, data = ret_perc, solver = "hybrid")

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Rolling Forecast Design
The GJR-GARCH model is evaluated using one-step-ahead rolling volatility forecasts. The initial estimation sample contains approximately 70% of the observations, with the remaining 30% used for forecast evaluation. Parameters are re-estimated every five observations using a moving estimation window.


Click to expand code
# window sized is determined and the refit period is set to be 5 days. 
window_size <- round(length(ret_perc) * 0.7)
refit_period <- 5

# rolling window forecast using rugarch 
roll_wind <- ugarchroll(
  spec            = spec_gjrg11,
  data            = ret_perc, 
  n.ahead         = 1,
  forecast.length = length(ret_perc) - window_size,
  refit.every     = refit_period,
  refit.window    = "moving",
  solver          = "hybrid"
)

# Extract predictions
fc_gjrgarch <- as.data.frame(roll_wind)

# Calculate variance and the realized proxy (squared returns)
var_fc_gjrgarch  <- fc_gjrgarch$Sigma^2
realised_proxy <- fc_gjrgarch$Realized^2


Conditional variance is not directly observable, so squared realised returns are used as a proxy. This proxy is noisy and includes the contribution of the conditional mean; squared forecast errors would align more directly with conditional variance when the mean is non-zero.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Forecast Evaluation
Forecast performance is assessed using mean squared error (MSE) and a QLIKE loss:
\[
\operatorname{MSE}
=
\frac{1}{H}
\sum_{t=1}^{H}
\left(v_t-\widehat{\sigma}_t^2\right)^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{QLIKE}
=
\frac{1}{H}
\sum_{t=1}^{H}
\left[
\ln\left(\widehat{\sigma}_t^2\right)
+
\frac{v_t}{\widehat{\sigma}_t^2}
\right],
\]
where (v_t) is the squared-return proxy and (H) is the number of forecast observations. Lower values indicate better performance when comparing forecasts evaluated on the same observations and scale.


Click to expand code
# computes average loss metrics in the functions
# Returns the mean of the loss series
compute_loss_metrics <- function(realized_proxy, var_fc) {
  eps = 1e-8  
  safe_var = pmax(var_fc, eps)
  
  mse_loss   = (realized_proxy - safe_var)^2
  qlike_loss = log(safe_var) + (realized_proxy / safe_var)
  
  data.frame(
    Mean_MSE   = mean(mse_loss), 
    Mean_QLIKE = mean(qlike_loss)
  )
}

 
loss_gjrgarch = compute_loss_metrics(realised_proxy, var_fc_gjrgarch)

loss_gjrgarch |>
  kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Rolling Forecast Losses for GJR-GARCH(1,1)"
  )



Rolling Forecast Losses for GJR-GARCH(1,1)


Mean_MSE
Mean_QLIKE




7.086
1.068





The mean MSE is 7.086, and the mean QLIKE is 1.068. The previously reported values were approximately 7.08 and 1.068, respectively.
These values summarize the forecast losses but do not establish whether forecasting performance is strong without a benchmark. Comparing GJR-GARCH with the other specifications or a simple variance forecast would provide a clearer assessment.
Although these forecasts are generated sequentially, the model specification was selected using the full dataset. A stricter out-of-sample assessment would select the specification using only the initial training sample before evaluating forecasts on the remaining observations.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Purpose and Design
A simulation study is conducted to examine how GARCH(1,1) parameter estimation changes with sample size. Unlike the earlier first-principles implementation, this simulation uses rugarch for both data generation and model estimation.
The study assesses finite-sample bias, variability, and numerical convergence. It does not prove estimator consistency, although improving parameter recovery as the sample size increases would be consistent with the expected large-sample behaviour.
The data-generating model has a zero mean, normally distributed standardized innovations, and the following parameters:
\[
\omega = 0.05,
\qquad
\alpha = 0.08,
\qquad
\beta = 0.88.
\]
Its persistence is (0.96), which is below one. Three sample sizes are considered: 250, 500, and 2,000 observations. Each setting is replicated 500 times, and the random seed is set to 123 for reproducibility.


Click to expand code
# true values for the synthetic example
omega_true <- 0.05
alpha_true <- 0.08
beta_true  <- 0.88

# true model specification
true_spec <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model     = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = FALSE),
  fixed.pars     = list(omega = omega_true, alpha1 = alpha_true, beta1 = beta_true),
  distribution.model = "norm"
)

# sample sizes tested to determine that the estimate function works for for different sample sizes
sample_sizes <- c(250, 500, 2000)
n_replications <- 500

run_simulation <- function(n_obs, n_reps, true_spec) {
  results <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_reps, ncol = 4)
  colnames(results) <- c("converged", "omega", "alpha1", "beta1")
  
  fit_spec <- ugarchspec(
    variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
    mean.model     = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = FALSE),
    distribution.model = "norm"
  )
  
  for (i in 1:n_reps) {
    sim = ugarchpath(true_spec, n.sim = n_obs)
    sim_returns =  as.numeric(fitted(sim))
    
    # Estimates model with error handling
    fit <- tryCatch(
      ugarchfit(fit_spec, data = sim_returns, solver = "hybrid"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    
    # convergence check 
    if (!is.null(fit) && convergence(fit) == 0) {
      pars <- coef(fit)
      results[i, ] <- c(1, pars["omega"], pars["alpha1"], pars["beta1"])
    } else {
      results[i, ] <- c(0, NA, NA, NA)
    }
  }
  
  dat <- as.data.frame(results)
  dat$N <- n_obs
  return(dat)
}

# running of simulations
set.seed(123)
sim_results <- bind_rows(lapply(sample_sizes, run_simulation, n_reps = n_replications, true_spec = true_spec))

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Bias, Variability, and Convergence
For each sample size, the convergence rate is calculated as the percentage of successful estimations. Bias is estimated as the average parameter estimate minus its true value, while the standard deviation measures variation across replications.
Where estimation fails, bias and standard deviation are calculated using only the converged fits.


Click to expand code
summary_stats <- sim_results %>%
  group_by(N) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Reps   = n(),
    Convergence_Rate = mean(converged) * 100,
    
    # bias of estimates
    Bias_Omega  = mean(omega, na.rm = TRUE) - omega_true,
    Bias_Alpha  = mean(alpha1, na.rm = TRUE) - alpha_true,
    Bias_Beta   = mean(beta1, na.rm = TRUE) - beta_true,
    
    # standard deviation of the estimates
    SD_Omega    = sd(omega, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_Alpha    = sd(alpha1, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_Beta     = sd(beta1, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

summary_stats |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "GARCH(1,1) Parameter Recovery Across Sample Sizes"
  )

In the reported results, all simulations converged. The absolute bias of the variance intercept decreases as the sample size increases.
The reaction coefficient, \(\alpha\), is underestimated in the smaller samples and becomes overestimated as the sample size increases, although the absolute bias becomes smaller. The persistence coefficient, \(\beta\), is underestimated across the sample sizes, with the magnitude of the bias also decreasing.
The standard deviations of all three parameter estimates decline as the sample size increases. Overall, the results suggest that larger samples improve estimation precision and bring the estimates closer to their true values under the specification considered.

title: A Comparative Study of GARCH Models for JSE Top 40 Volatility
text:
Sampling Distributions
Box plots illustrate how the distributions of the parameter estimates change with sample size. Dashed horizontal lines indicate the true parameter values.


Click to expand code
# table created for the true values 
true_vals <- data.frame(
  Parameter  = c("omega", "alpha1", "beta1"),
  True_Value = c(omega_true, alpha_true, beta_true)

# data manipulation of the results so that plotting can occur

  filter(converged == 1) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(omega, alpha1, beta1), names_to = "Parameter", values_to = "Estimate")

# box-plot of each parameter value for each of the simulated datasets
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = factor(N), y = Estimate, fill = factor(N))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(data = true_vals, aes(yintercept = True_Value), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +

  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "GARCH(1,1) Sampling Distributions Across Sample Sizes (N)",
    x = "Sample Size (N)",
    y = "Parameter Estimate",
    fill = "Sample Size"
  )









The narrowing distributions provide visual evidence of improved precision in larger samples. These findings apply to the chosen parameter values and normally distributed innovations. Further simulations would be needed to assess whether the same patterns hold under different persistence levels, innovation distributions, or model misspecification.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Crime and socioeconomic inequality are important concerns in South Africa. Research on crime often examines factors associated with criminal activity, but understanding how recorded crime changes over time is also important for identifying trends and producing forecasts.
This project uses time series methods to examine four categories of recorded crime in South Africa: murder, aggravated robbery, residential burglary, and vehicle theft. ARIMA models describe and forecast each crime series using its own historical behaviour, while ARIMAX models incorporate GDP, inflation, and unemployment as explanatory variables.
The project addresses two main questions:

How have recorded crime counts changed over time in South Africa?
Do macroeconomic indicators help explain and forecast changes in recorded crime counts?

The analysis focuses on recorded cases rather than population-adjusted crime rates. It examines associations between aggregate variables and does not establish that these variables cause crime or explain an individual’s likelihood of committing an offence.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Data Sources and Variables
The response variables are the annual numbers of cases recorded by the South African Police Service (SAPS) for four crime categories:

Murder.
Aggravated robbery.
Residential burglary.
Vehicle theft.

These figures represent recorded offences rather than all crimes committed. Changes in the series may therefore reflect changes in criminal activity, reporting behaviour, or recording practices.
The explanatory variables are GDP, inflation, and the unemployment rate. The datasets are aggregated and joined using a common year identifier. The intended study period is 2005–2025, giving 21 annual observations where all years are available across the datasets.
The crime data are supplied as aggregated counts, and no individual-level personal information is used in this analysis.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Loading Packages
The following packages are used to import and clean the data, construct time series objects, estimate models, and present the results.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Importing Crime Data
The crime dataset records reporting periods using labels such as 2005/2006. The first year of each reporting period is used as its year identifier. Thus, the label 2005 represents the reporting period 2005/2006 rather than the calendar year 2005.
The selected crime categories are summed across the records within each reporting period.


Click to expand code
# importing crime data and aggregating annually
crime_dat <- read_csv("sapacr-2005-2026-v1.5.csv")
crime_cols <- c("murder", "aggr_robbery", "burglary_res", "vehicle_theft")

crime_annual <- crime_dat |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(substr(year, 1, 4))) |> # the data has dates as e.g. 2005/2006 and therefore it is chosen to be 2005
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(crime_cols), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))


This aggregation assumes that the source rows represent non-overlapping units. Any national or provincial totals included alongside their component records would need to be excluded to avoid double counting.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Preparing the Inflation Series
The CPI data require additional preparation because they are stored in two Excel files with overlapping dates. Each file is reshaped into a monthly series containing a date and an index value.
The overlapping observations are then used to calculate a scaling factor so that the two index series can be joined on a common numerical basis. This adjustment assumes that the selected series are conceptually comparable; rescaling alone cannot resolve differences in their coverage or definition.


Click to expand code
# importing cpi dataset
read_cpi_index <- function(path, code, headline_only = FALSE) {
  r = read_excel(path) |> filter(H03 == code)
  if (headline_only) r <- r |> filter(H04 == "CPI Headline")   # for the new file
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
  r |>
    select(starts_with("MO")) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "col", values_to = "index") |>
    mutate(
      date  = make_date(as.integer(substr(col, 5, 8)), as.integer(substr(col, 3, 4)), 1),
      index = as.numeric(index)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(index)) |>
    select(date, index)
}

old <- read_cpi_index("cpi-2000-2008-v1.xlsx", "VPN00000")
new <- read_cpi_index("cpi-2008-2026-v1.1.xlsx", "CPS00000", headline_only = TRUE)
# joining both cpi datasets into 1 
overlap <- inner_join(old, new, by = "date", suffix = c("_old", "_new"))
nrow(overlap) # 4 rows overlapping


[1] 2


Click to expand code
scale <- mean(overlap$index_old / overlap$index_new)

cpi_idx <- bind_rows(old, new |> filter(!date %in% old$date) |> mutate(index = index * scale)) |>
  arrange(date)

range(cpi_idx$date)                             


[1] "2000-01-01" "2026-06-01"


Click to expand code
cpi_idx |> 
  mutate(gap = lubridate::interval(lag(date), date) %/% months(1)) |> 
  filter(gap > 1)  


# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: date <date>, index <dbl>, gap <dbl>


Monthly year-on-year inflation is calculated as
\[
\pi_t
=
100\left(
\frac{I_t}{I_{t-12}}-1
\right),
\]
where (I_t) is the CPI index in month (t).
The monthly inflation rates are averaged over April–March financial years. Only financial years with 12 available monthly inflation observations are retained.


Click to expand code
# ensuring cpi is matched properly
cpi_m <- cpi_idx |>
  mutate(infl = 100 * (index / index[match(date %m-% months(12), date)] - 1)) |>
  filter(!is.na(infl))

# funtion to help mutate date data
to_fy <- function(d) if_else(month(d) >= 4, year(d), year(d) - 1L)
# aggregating to annual
cpi_annual <- cpi_m |>
  mutate(Year = to_fy(date)) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  filter(n() == 12) |>
  summarise(CPI = mean(infl))


Although the variable is named CPI in the code, it contains the average year-on-year inflation rate, expressed as a percentage, rather than the CPI index level.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Combining and Checking the Data
The crime counts and macroeconomic variables are joined using their year identifiers. Inner joins retain only the years that are present in every dataset.


Click to expand code
# combine into 1 dataset and convert to a tsibble object (time series)
crime_data <- crime_annual |>
  inner_join(gdp_annual,   by = "Year") |>
  inner_join(unemp_annual, by = "Year") |>
  inner_join(cpi_annual,   by = "Year") |>
  as_tsibble(index = Year)

# missing values checked
sum(is.na(crime_data))  


[1] 0


Click to expand code
# checks
range(crime_data$Year)


[1] 2005 2025


Click to expand code
nrow(crime_data)   


[1] 21


The combined dataset contains 21 annual observations, covering year labels from 2005 to 2025. There are 0 missing values in the retained dataset.
No imputation is applied. However, the absence of missing values after joining does not establish that every source dataset was complete: inner joins can remove unmatched years, and the aggregation functions omit missing source values when calculating totals or averages.
There is also a timing limitation. Crime and inflation are organised by reporting or financial year, while GDP and unemployment are averaged by calendar year. Matching the same year labels therefore does not align the underlying periods exactly. These periods should ideally be harmonised before interpreting the ARIMAX coefficients or evaluating predictive relationships.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Recorded Crime Counts


Click to expand code
crimes <- c("murder", "aggr_robbery", "burglary_res", "vehicle_theft")
regs   <- c("GDP", "CPI", "Unemployment")

# time series plots 
# function for plotting
c1 <- crime_data |> autoplot(murder, colour = "red") + labs(title = "Murder", y = NULL)
c2 <- crime_data |> autoplot(aggr_robbery, colour = "orange") + labs(title = "Aggravated robbery", y = NULL)
c3 <- crime_data |> autoplot(burglary_res, colour = "blue") + labs(title = "Residential burglary", y = NULL)
c4 <- crime_data |> autoplot(vehicle_theft, colour = "green") + labs(title = "Vehicle theft", y = NULL)

(c1 | c2) / (c3 | c4) + plot_annotation(title = "Crime series")









The murder series shows an upward movement over much of the later study period, interrupted by a decline around 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Recorded cases subsequently rise and appear to peak around the reporting periods labelled 2022–2023 before declining towards the end of the series.
Aggravated robbery follows a less consistent pattern. Recorded cases decline around 2010–2012 before increasing again. A further dip is visible around 2020, followed by a recovery and a more recent decline after approximately 2022–2023.
Residential burglary and vehicle theft both display broadly declining trends over the study period. Both also show a decrease around the pandemic period, although the longer-term downward movement extends beyond this disruption.
The movements around 2020 coincide with the COVID-19 pandemic and associated restrictions. These restrictions may have affected opportunities for particular offences, mobility, and reporting behaviour. However, the plots alone cannot establish the reasons for the observed changes.
The differences between the four series suggest that each crime category may require a different time series specification. A model suitable for a declining property-crime series may not adequately describe the changing pattern of recorded murder cases.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Macroeconomic Indicators
The explanatory variables are plotted below to examine their long-term movements and any disruptions that may be relevant to the crime series.


Click to expand code
r1 <- crime_data |> autoplot(GDP, colour = "purple") + labs(title = "GDP", y = NULL)
r2 <- crime_data |> autoplot(CPI, colour = "darkgreen") + labs(title = "CPI (inflation, %)", y = NULL)
r3 <- crime_data |> autoplot(Unemployment, colour = "brown") + labs(title = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = NULL)

(r1 | r2 | r3) + plot_annotation(title = "Macroeconomic regressors")









The GDP series shows a broad upward movement, with disruptions around the 2008–2009 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. These events provide economic context for changes in the series. However, the interpretation of its upward trend depends on whether the source measures nominal or real GDP, which should be confirmed before drawing conclusions about growth in economic activity.
Inflation fluctuates rather than following a sustained upward trend. The series shows a pronounced increase around 2008 and further movements during the pandemic and subsequent recovery period. More recent observations appear to indicate easing inflation. These changes describe movements in the rate of price increases rather than changes in the CPI index level itself.
The unemployment rate displays a broad upward trend over much of the study period, with particularly high levels around the pandemic and its aftermath. A modest decline is visible in the later observations, although unemployment remains elevated relative to earlier years.
These patterns motivate examining whether macroeconomic indicators add useful information to forecasts based on past crime counts alone. Nevertheless, visual co-movement does not establish a statistical relationship or causation. Trends, possible structural changes, and the short sample of annual observations must be considered when specifying and interpreting the models.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation
The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures the relationship between a series and its past values. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures the relationship at each lag after accounting for the intervening lags.
These plots provide an initial assessment of persistence in the recorded crime series. However, model orders should not be selected from these plots alone before assessing stationarity.


Click to expand code
# acf plots for crimes 
p1 <- crime_data |> ACF(murder, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: murder")
p2 <- crime_data |> ACF(aggr_robbery, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: aggravated robbery")
p3 <- crime_data |> ACF(burglary_res, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: residential burglary")
p4 <- crime_data |> ACF(vehicle_theft, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: vehicle theft")
# layout for acf plots
(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4)









Click to expand code
# acf plots for explanatory
q1 <- crime_data |> PACF(murder, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: murder")
q2 <- crime_data |> PACF(aggr_robbery, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: aggravated robbery")
q3 <- crime_data |> PACF(burglary_res, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: residential burglary")
q4 <- crime_data |> PACF(vehicle_theft, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: vehicle theft")
# layout for acf plots
(q1 | q2) / (q3 | q4)









The ACF plots show positive autocorrelation that gradually declines as the lag increases. Significant spikes extend approximately to lag three for residential burglary and vehicle theft, and to lag two for murder and aggravated robbery. Lag one has the strongest autocorrelation in each series.
In the PACF plots, the main significant spike occurs at lag one across all four crime categories. These patterns indicate persistence, but they may also reflect non-stationarity. Stationarity is therefore assessed before using the correlation patterns to identify candidate ARIMA models.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Preliminary Cross-Correlation Analysis
The cross-correlation function (CCF) measures the association between two series at different lags. It is used here to explore potential relationships between recorded crime counts and the macroeconomic indicators.
The variable named CPI contains the inflation rate calculated from CPI rather than the CPI index level.


Click to expand code
# murder and aggravated robbery ccf plots
a1 <- crime_data |> CCF(murder, GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Murder & GDP")
a2 <- crime_data |> CCF(murder, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Murder & CPI")
a3 <- crime_data |> CCF(murder, Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Murder & Unemployment")

b1 <- crime_data |> CCF(aggr_robbery, GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Aggravated robbery & GDP")
b2 <- crime_data |> CCF(aggr_robbery, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Aggravated robbery & CPI")
b3 <- crime_data |> CCF(aggr_robbery, Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Aggravated robbery & Unemployment")
# ccf plot layout
(a1 | a2 | a3) / (b1 | b2 | b3)









The preliminary plots suggest associations between murder and both GDP and unemployment. For aggravated robbery, all three macroeconomic indicators display potentially relevant correlations, including an isolated significant correlation with inflation.


Click to expand code
# burglary and vehicle theft ccf plots
d1 <- crime_data |> CCF(burglary_res, GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Residential burglary & GDP")
d2 <- crime_data |> CCF(burglary_res, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Residential burglary & CPI")
d3 <- crime_data |> CCF(burglary_res, Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Residential burglary & Unemployment")

e1 <- crime_data |> CCF(vehicle_theft, GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Vehicle theft & GDP")
e2 <- crime_data |> CCF(vehicle_theft, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Vehicle theft & CPI")
e3 <- crime_data |> CCF(vehicle_theft, Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Vehicle theft & Unemployment")
# ccf plot layout
(d1 | d2 | d3) / (e1 | e2 | e3)









GDP and unemployment appear to be potential explanatory variables for residential burglary. For vehicle theft, all three indicators display potentially relevant correlations.
These findings are preliminary. Correlations between non-stationary series can arise from shared trends rather than a meaningful relationship. Serial dependence within each series can also affect the CCF. The relationships are therefore reassessed after examining stationarity and applying the required transformations.
These full-sample plots are descriptive. Predictor and model selection for forecast evaluation will rely on on the training sample to avoid using information from the test period.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Training and Test Sets
The dataset is divided chronologically into a training sample and a test sample. The training sample contains 18 annual observations from 2005 to 2022, while the test sample contains three observations from 2023 to 2025. This corresponds to approximately 86% of the observations for training and 14% for testing.
The training data are used to assess stationarity, identify candidate models, and estimate their parameters. The test data are reserved for evaluating forecasts.


Click to expand code
# splitting into training and test

n_test <- 3
train_data <- crime_data |> filter(Year <= max(Year) - n_test)
test_data  <- crime_data |> filter(Year >  max(Year) - n_test)

# no of obs
nrow(train_data)

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Stationarity Assessment
Stationarity is assessed using the KPSS test and the recommended number of differences returned by unitroot_ndiffs().
For the KPSS test, the hypotheses are:

(H_0): The series is stationary under the test specification.
(H_1): The series is not stationary under the test specification.

A small KPSS p-value provides evidence against stationarity. This interpretation differs from unit-root tests whose null hypothesis is the presence of a unit root.


Click to expand code
# test for differencing and whether te time series plots are stationary 
# response variables
train_data |> features(murder,        list(unitroot_kpss, unitroot_ndiffs))

The reported KPSS results give small p-values for murder, residential burglary, and vehicle theft, providing evidence against stationarity. The differencing procedure recommends one difference for each of these series.
For aggravated robbery, the results do not indicate that differencing is required.
Among the explanatory variables, GDP and unemployment also require one difference. Inflation does not require differencing under the procedure used.
These findings guide the initial transformations, although stationarity tests have limited power in a training sample of only 18 annual observations.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
First Differencing
First differencing is applied to the series identified above:
\[
\Delta y_t = y_t-y_{t-1}.
\]
For crime counts, this transformation measures the annual change in recorded cases. For unemployment, it measures the change in the unemployment rate in percentage points. The GDP difference measures an absolute change in the source units rather than a percentage growth rate.


Click to expand code
# difference the series that required differencing
train_diff <- train_data |>
  mutate(
    d_murder        = difference(murder),
    d_burglary_res  = difference(burglary_res),
    d_vehicle_theft = difference(vehicle_theft),
    d_GDP           = difference(GDP),
    d_Unemployment  = difference(Unemployment)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(d_murder))      # drops the first year as it is NA

# checks for stationarity of the difference ones
train_diff |> features(d_murder,        list(unitroot_kpss, unitroot_ndiffs))


# A tibble: 1 × 3
  kpss_stat kpss_pvalue ndiffs
      <dbl>       <dbl>  <int>

After first differencing, the reported results recommend no further differencing, and the KPSS tests no longer reject stationarity at the chosen significance level.
These results support proceeding with the transformed series, although failure to reject the stationarity null does not prove stationarity.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
ACF and PACF After Transformation
The ACF and PACF are examined again using the differenced series where required. Aggravated robbery remains in levels because the stationarity assessment did not recommend differencing.


Click to expand code
# acf & pacf plots  for crimes
p1 <- train_diff |> ACF(d_murder, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: d(murder)")
p2 <- train_diff |> ACF(aggr_robbery, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: aggravated robbery")
p3 <- train_diff |> ACF(d_burglary_res, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: d(residential burglary)")
p4 <- train_diff |> ACF(d_vehicle_theft, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF: d(vehicle theft)")

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4)









Click to expand code
q1 <- train_diff |> PACF(d_murder, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: d(murder)")
q2 <- train_diff |> PACF(aggr_robbery, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: aggravated robbery")
q3 <- train_diff |> PACF(d_burglary_res, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: d(residential burglary)")
q4 <- train_diff |> PACF(d_vehicle_theft, lag_max = 8) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF: d(vehicle theft)")

(q1 | q2) / (q3 | q4)









For differenced murder and residential burglary, neither the ACF nor the PACF shows a clear significant pattern. This suggests ARIMA(0,1,0) as a useful initial candidate for each original series.
For aggravated robbery, the ACF and PACF both show a prominent spike at lag one. This motivates considering low-order AR, MA, and combined ARMA specifications. A gradual decline in the ACF alone does not establish an MA(1) model; the cutoff and decay patterns in both plots must be considered together.
For differenced vehicle theft, neither plot shows a clear significant pattern. ARIMA(0,1,0) is therefore a natural initial candidate, while ARIMA(0,1,1) can be evaluated as an alternative.
The proposed baseline candidates are:



Crime category
Initial model candidates




Murder
ARIMA(0,1,0)


Aggravated robbery
ARIMA(1,0,0), ARIMA(0,0,1), and ARIMA(1,0,1)


Residential burglary
ARIMA(0,1,0)


Vehicle theft
ARIMA(0,1,0) and ARIMA(0,1,1)



These are candidate specifications rather than confirmed final models. Information criteria, residual diagnostics, and forecast performance are needed to assess their suitability. Intercept or drift terms must also be considered when fitting the models.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025
text:
Cross-Correlation After Transformation
The CCF is reassessed using the training data after the required transformations. These plots examine relationships between changes in the non-stationary series and the variables retained in levels.
The differenced variables are used here for exploratory analysis. Their use in the final ARIMAX specification must be considered separately from the differencing applied to the model’s errors.

Murder and Aggravated Robbery


Click to expand code
# ccf plots for murder and robbery
a1 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_murder, d_GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Murder) & d(GDP)")
a2 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_murder, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Murder) & CPI")
a3 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_murder, d_Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Murder) & d(Unemployment)")

b1 <- train_diff |> CCF(aggr_robbery, d_GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Agg. robbery & d(GDP)")
b2 <- train_diff |> CCF(aggr_robbery, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Agg. robbery & CPI")
b3 <- train_diff |> CCF(aggr_robbery, d_Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Agg. robbery & d(Unemployment)")

(a1 | a2 | a3) / (b1 | b2 | b3)









For murder, the reported plots show:

A negative correlation with the change in GDP at plotted lag −1 and a positive correlation at lag zero.
A negative correlation with inflation at plotted lag −2.
A positive correlation with the change in unemployment at lag zero.

For aggravated robbery, the main reported correlations are negative associations with inflation at plotted lags −2, −3, and −4. The earlier apparent associations with GDP and unemployment are less evident after transformation.
The lag labels are reported as displayed rather than interpreted automatically as predictor delays. Their direction depends on the CCF convention and the order of the variables supplied to the function. This must be checked before constructing lagged predictors.


Residential Burglary and Vehicle Theft


Click to expand code
# ccf plots for burglary and vehicle theft
d1 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_burglary_res, d_GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Burglary) & d(GDP)")
d2 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_burglary_res, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Burglary) & CPI")
d3 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_burglary_res, d_Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Burglary) & d(Unemployment)")

e1 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_vehicle_theft, d_GDP, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Vehicle theft) & d(GDP)")
e2 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_vehicle_theft, CPI, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Vehicle theft) & CPI")
e3 <- train_diff |> CCF(d_vehicle_theft, d_Unemployment, lag_max = 4) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "d(Vehicle theft) & d(Unemployment)")

(d1 | d2 | d3) / (e1 | e2 | e3)









For residential burglary, the reported plots show positive correlations with inflation and the change in GDP at lag zero. A negative correlation with the change in unemployment appears at plotted lag one.
For vehicle theft, a positive correlation with the change in GDP appears at lag zero, while a negative correlation with the change in unemployment appears at plotted lag one. Inflation does not show a clear significant relationship after transformation.
These findings identify possible relationships for further investigation, but they do not establish causation or guarantee that the variables will improve forecasts. Differencing also does not remove all serial dependence; prewhitening could provide a more reliable assessment of cross-correlations.
Given the small sample and the number of correlations examined, isolated significant spikes should be interpreted cautiously. Parsimonious ARIMAX specifications are therefore preferred. Any contemporaneous or future explanatory values required for forecasting must also be available at the forecast origin or supplied through forecasts or explicit scenarios.

title: Forecasting Crime in South Africa: An ARIMA and ARIMAX Analysis of Macroeconomic Indicators, 2005–2025

In-Sample Model Comparison
The candidate models are compared using AIC, corrected AIC (AICc), and BIC. These criteria balance model fit against complexity, with lower values indicating a more favourable balance.
AICc is used as the main ranking criterion because the training sample is small. Nevertheless, models with several explanatory variables require particular caution when only 18 annual observations are available.

title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
State-space models are used to represent dynamic systems in which the true underlying process, or data-generating process (DGP), cannot be observed directly. Instead, the underlying process is represented by a latent state, while the available observations contain measurement noise. The objective is therefore to estimate the unobserved state using the noisy information that is available.
The Kalman filter is a recursive technique used for filtering, forecasting, and estimating latent states in linear Gaussian state-space models. It follows a Bayesian approach in which prior information about the state is combined with new observations to produce an updated estimate. At each time step, the Kalman filter first predicts the current state using the information available from the previous time step. Once a new observation becomes available, this prediction is updated according to the uncertainty associated with both the underlying process and the observed measurement. This produces a posterior estimate of the latent state.
For example, consider the simple local-level state-space model:
\[
x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t,
\]
where
\[
w_t \sim N(0,Q),
\]
and the observation equation
\[
y_t = x_t + v_t,
\]
where
\[
v_t \sim N(0,R).
\]
Here, \(x_t\) represents the true latent state at time \(t\), while \(y_t\) represents the observed measurement. The term \(w_t\) represents process noise, with variance \(Q\), while \(v_t\) represents measurement noise, with variance \(R\).
The model therefore contains two distinct sources of uncertainty. A large value of \(Q\) indicates greater uncertainty in the evolution of the underlying state, meaning that the true state may change substantially between consecutive time periods. In contrast, a large value of \(R\) indicates greater measurement uncertainty, meaning that the observed values may contain substantial noise and may therefore be less reliable representations of the true state.
The Kalman filter must account for these two sources of uncertainty when determining how much weight should be placed on the predicted state relative to the newly observed measurement. Understanding how the filter behaves under different levels and forms of uncertainty is therefore important when applying it to dynamic systems.
This honours project aims to answer the following research question:
How do different forms of uncertainty and disruption affect the ability of a Kalman filter to estimate an unobserved dynamic state?


The Kalman filter is a recursive algorithm that follows a Bayesian approach by continuously updating the estimated state as new observations become available. A key component of the algorithm is the Kalman gain, which determines how much weight should be given to the new observation relative to the predicted state, based on their respective levels of uncertainty.
The first step of the Kalman filter is the prediction step. The current state is predicted using the estimated state from the previous time period. The uncertainty associated with this prediction is also calculated by incorporating the process uncertainty.
Once a new observation becomes available, the difference between the observed value and the predicted value is calculated. This difference is known as the innovation or prediction error, and it represents the new information provided by the observation.
The Kalman gain is then calculated using the uncertainty associated with the predicted state and the measurement uncertainty. The gain determines how much the predicted state should be adjusted in response to the new observation. When the observation is relatively reliable, greater weight is placed on the new information. In contrast, when measurement uncertainty is high, the filter places greater weight on the predicted state.
Finally, the predicted state is updated using the Kalman gain and the innovation to obtain the new estimate of the latent state. The uncertainty associated with the state estimate is also updated. This updated state and its uncertainty are then used as the starting point for the prediction at the next time period.



The first step of the analysis was to create a baseline simulation using a simple local-level state-space model. The purpose of this simulation is to establish how the Kalman filter behaves under controlled conditions before introducing more complex scenarios involving different levels of uncertainty, model misspecification, structural changes, and missing observations.
A sample size of \(n=250\) observations was used. The process variance and measurement variance were initially set to
\(Q=2\)
and
\(R=1.5\).
The simulated data follow the local-level state-space model introduced previously. The state equation is
\[
x_t=x_{t-1}+w_t,
\]
where
\[
w_t\sim N(0,Q),
\]
and the observation equation is
\[
y_t=x_t+v_t,
\]
where
\[
v_t\sim N(0,R).
\]
Here, \(x_t\) represents the true latent state at time \(t\), while \(y_t\) represents the observed measurement. The process error \(w_t\) determines how the underlying latent state evolves between consecutive time periods, while the measurement error \(v_t\) introduces noise into the observed values.
Therefore, \(Q\) represents the process variance, while \(R\) represents the measurement variance. For the baseline simulation, \(Q=2\) allows the latent state to vary over time, while \(R=1.5\) introduces measurement uncertainty around the true state.
The relationship between the latent states, observations, and the two sources of uncertainty can be represented using the following directed acyclic graph (DAG):
The DAG illustrates that each latent state \(x_t\) depends on the previous state \(x_{t-1}\) and the process noise \(w_t\). Each observed value \(y_t\) then depends on the corresponding latent state \(x_t\) and measurement noise \(v_t\).
Since the data are simulated, the true latent state is known. This provides an important advantage for the simulation study because the state estimates produced by the Kalman filter can be directly compared with the true underlying process.
The simulated latent state and noisy observations are shown below.

# data simulated

set.seed(432)

# parameters
n <- 250 
Q <- 2
R <- 1.5
x0 <- 0 

# inialize xt and yt 
yt <- numeric(n)
xt <- numeric(n)

xt[1] <- x0

# loop for simulated latent variable 
for (i in 2:n){
  wt = rnorm(1, mean = 0 , sd = sqrt(Q))
  xt[i] = xt[i-1] + wt
}

# loop for observed state
for (i in 1:n){
  vt = rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(R))
  yt[i] = xt[i] + vt 
}

  geom_line(aes(y = True_State, colour = "True latent state"),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Observed, colour = "Observed process"),
            linewidth = 0.7,
            alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "True Latent State and Observed Process",
    subtitle = "Baseline simulation with Q = 2 and R = 1.5",
    x = "Time",
    y = "State",
    colour = "Series"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The plot below shows the simulated true latent process and the corresponding observed state. The observed values generally follow the movement of the underlying latent process; however, they fluctuate around the true state due to the presence of measurement noise. As a result, the observations do not provide a perfect representation of the true latent state. This demonstrates the state-estimation problem that the Kalman filter aims to address by using the noisy observations to estimate the underlying process more accurately.



Following the baseline simulation, the Kalman filter was implemented from first principles rather than relying initially on an existing filtering function. This was done to demonstrate the recursive calculations underlying the algorithm and to examine how information and uncertainty are propagated through the filtering process.
For the local-level model, an initial estimate of the state and its associated uncertainty must first be specified. The Kalman filter then proceeds recursively through prediction and update steps for each observation.
At time \(t\), the previous filtered state estimate is used to predict the current latent state:
\[
\hat{x}_{t|t-1}=\hat{x}_{t-1|t-1}.
\]
The uncertainty associated with this prediction is also updated by incorporating the process variance:
\[
P_{t|t-1}=P_{t-1|t-1}+Q.
\]
This reflects the fact that uncertainty increases as the underlying process evolves between consecutive time periods.


Once the new observation \(y_t\) becomes available, the difference between the observed value and the predicted state is calculated:
\[
e_t=y_t-\hat{x}_{t|t-1}.
\]
This quantity is known as the innovation, or prediction error, and represents the new information provided by the observation.
The variance of the innovation is:
\[
S_t=P_{t|t-1}+R.
\]
It incorporates uncertainty from both the predicted state and the measurement process.



The Kalman gain determines how strongly the predicted state should be adjusted in response to the new observation:
\[
K_t=
\frac{P_{t|t-1}}
{P_{t|t-1}+R}.
\]
The Kalman gain therefore depends on the relative uncertainty associated with the predicted state and the observed measurement. When measurement uncertainty \(R\) is large, less weight is placed on the observation. In contrast, when the predicted state is relatively uncertain compared with the measurement, greater weight is placed on the new observation.



The predicted state is then corrected using the innovation and the Kalman gain:
\[
\hat{x}_{t|t} = \hat{x}_{t|t-1}
+
K_te_t.
\]
The updated estimate therefore combines information from the model prediction with information contained in the new observation.



Finally, the uncertainty associated with the filtered state is updated:
\[
P_{t|t} = (1-K_t)P_{t|t-1}.
\]
The updated state estimate \(\hat{x}_{t|t}\) and its uncertainty \(P_{t|t}\) then become the inputs for the prediction step at time \(t+1\). This recursive process is repeated for all 250 observations.


Click to expand code
kalman_filt <- function(y, Q, R, m0, P0){
  
  # initialize vectors 
  N = length(y)
  
  at = numeric(N)
  Rt = numeric(N)
  Qt = numeric(N)
  mt = numeric(N)
  Pt = numeric(N)
  et = numeric(N)
  Kt = numeric(N)
  
  # loop for filter
  for(i in 1:N){
    
    # prediction
    if(i == 1){
      at[i] = m0
      Rt[i] = P0 + Q
    } else {
      at[i] = mt[i-1]
      Rt[i] = Pt[i-1] + Q
    }
    
    # innovation 
    et[i] = y[i] - at[i]
    Qt[i] = Rt[i] + R
    
    # Kalman gain
    Kt[i] = Rt[i] / Qt[i]
    
    # update states
    mt[i] = at[i] + Kt[i] * et[i]
    Pt[i] = (1 - Kt[i]) * Rt[i]
  }
  
  return(data.frame(
    Time = 1:N,
    Observation = y,
    Predicted_State = at,
    Prediction_Variance = Rt,
    Innovation = et,
    Innovation_Variance = Qt,
    Kalman_Gain = Kt,
    Filtered_State = mt,
    Filtered_Variance = Pt
  ))
}

# implement from the function 
kf_res <- kalman_filt(y = yt, Q = Q, R = R, m0 = 0, P0 = 1)






To validate the implementation, the manually calculated filtered state estimates were compared with estimates obtained using the dlm package. The same process variance, measurement variance, initial state estimate, and initial state uncertainty were specified to ensure that the two implementations were comparable.

{P_{t|t-1}+R}.
\]
The Kalman gain therefore depends on the relative uncertainty associated with the predicted state and the observed measurement. When measurement uncertainty \(R\) is large, less weight is placed on the observation. In contrast, when the predicted state is relatively uncertain compared with the measurement, greater weight is placed on the new observation.



The predicted state is then corrected using the innovation and the Kalman gain:
\[
\hat{x}_{t|t} = \hat{x}_{t|t-1}
+
K_te_t.
\]
The updated estimate therefore combines information from the model prediction with information contained in the new observation.



Finally, the uncertainty associated with the filtered state is updated:
\[
P_{t|t} = (1-K_t)P_{t|t-1}.
\]
The updated state estimate \(\hat{x}_{t|t}\) and its uncertainty \(P_{t|t}\) then become the inputs for the prediction step at time \(t+1\). This recursive process is repeated for all 250 observations.


Click to expand code
kalman_filt <- function(y, Q, R, m0, P0){
  
  # initialize vectors 
  N = length(y)
  
  at = numeric(N)
  Rt = numeric(N)
  Qt = numeric(N)
  mt = numeric(N)
  Pt = numeric(N)
  et = numeric(N)
  Kt = numeric(N)
  
  # loop for filter
  for(i in 1:N){
    
    # prediction
    if(i == 1){
      at[i] = m0
      Rt[i] = P0 + Q
    } else {
      at[i] = mt[i-1]
      Rt[i] = Pt[i-1] + Q
    }
    
    # innovation 
    et[i] = y[i] - at[i]
    Qt[i] = Rt[i] + R
    
    # Kalman gain
    Kt[i] = Rt[i] / Qt[i]
    
    # update states
    mt[i] = at[i] + Kt[i] * et[i]
    Pt[i] = (1 - Kt[i]) * Rt[i]
  }
  
  return(data.frame(
    Time = 1:N,
    Observation = y,
    Predicted_State = at,
    Prediction_Variance = Rt,
    Innovation = et,
    Innovation_Variance = Qt,
    Kalman_Gain = Kt,
    Filtered_State = mt,
    Filtered_Variance = Pt
  ))
}

# implement from the function 
kf_res <- kalman_filt(y = yt, Q = Q, R = R, m0 = 0, P0 = 1)

title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
Scenario 1: Measurement and Process Uncertainty
Measurement and process uncertainty both affect how the Kalman filter smooths the observations and updates its estimates. This scenario focuses on answering two questions:
How does measurement uncertainty affect state estimation?
How does uncertainty in the underlying process affect the responsiveness of the Kalman filter?
Both measurement and process uncertainties have a large effect of the values and ow the smooting works however the actual estiamtes is another story. This scanrio will focus on answering these 2 queations: 1. How does measurement uncertainty affect state estimation? 2. How does uncertainty in the underlying process affect the responsiveness of the Kalman filter?

Measurement Uncertainty
Measurement uncertainty was changed using three levels:
Low measurement uncertainty: (R=0.5)
Moderate measurement uncertainty: (R=1.5)
High measurement uncertainty: (R=6)
Process uncertainty \(Q\) is held constant at 2.


Click to expand code
R_vals <- c(
  low = 0.5,
  meoderate = 1.5,
  high = 6
)

# function to create true state values
simulate_state <- function(n, Q, R, x0 = 0){
  
  xt = numeric(n)
  yt = numeric(n)
  
  xt[1] = x0
  
  for(i in 2:n){
    wt = rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(Q))
    xt[i] = xt[i - 1] + wt
  }
  
  for(i in 1:n){
    vt = rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(R))
    yt[i] = xt[i] + vt
  }
  
  data.frame(
    Time = 1:n,
    True_State = xt,
    Observation = yt
  )
}


The three measurement uncertainty scenarios are then simulated and filtered.


Click to expand code
R_res <- data.frame()
set.seed(432)

for(i  in 1:3){
  
  sim <- simulate_state(
    n = 250,
    Q = 2,
    R = R_vals[i]
  )
  
  kf <- kalman_filt(
    y = sim$Observation,
    Q = 2,
    R = R_vals[i],
    m0 = 0,
    P0 = 1
  )
  
  temp <- data.frame(
    Time = sim$Time,
    True_State = sim$True_State,
    Observation = sim$Observation,
    Filtered_State = kf$Filtered_State,
    Kalman_Gain = kf$Kalman_Gain,
    R = R_vals[i]
  )
  
  measurement_results <- rbind(
    R_res,
    temp
  )
}


The performance measures and plots are shown below.

As measurement uncertainty increases, the observations become less reliable. The Kalman gain therefore decreases because the filter places less weight on the new observations and more weight on its predicted state.
This results in more smoothing as \(R\) increases. The estimation error can also become larger because the observations contain more noise and provide less accurate information about the true state. This shows how measurement uncertainty affects how much the Kalman filter trusts the observed values.


Process Uncertainty
Process uncertainty was changed using low, moderate and high values:
Low: (Q=0.2)
Moderate: (Q=2)
High: (Q=10)
Measurement uncertainty is held constant at (R=1.5).

  Moderate = 2,
  High = 10
)

set.seed(432)

for(i in 1:3){
  
  sim <- simulate_state(
    n = 250,
    Q = Q_vals[i],
    R = 1.5

  kf <- kalman_filt(

  temp <- data.frame(

    True_State = sim$True_State,
    Observation = sim$Observation,
    Filtered_State = kf$Filtered_State,
    Kalman_Gain = kf$Kalman_Gain,
    Q = Q_vals[i]
  )

    Q_results,
    temp
  )
}

  group_by(Q) |>
  summarise(

    MAE = MAE(True_State, Filtered_State),

The Kalman gain increases as \(Q\) increases. This makes sense because a larger \(Q\) means that there is more uncertainty about how the true state changes over time. The filter becomes less confident in its previous prediction and therefore places more weight on the new observation.
This shows the trade-off between smoothing and responsiveness. When \(Q\) is low, the filter assumes that the true state does not change too much between periods, so the estimates are smoother. When \(Q\) is high, the filter allows the state to change more and becomes more responsive to new observations.
The RMSE also increases in some of the higher-\(Q\) scenarios. However, increasing \(Q\) also makes the simulated true state more volatile, meaning that the state itself becomes more difficult to estimate.

The results show that the performance of the Kalman filter depends on both measurement and process uncertainty. Higher measurement uncertainty generally leads to larger errors because the observations contain more noise. Higher process uncertainty also makes the underlying state more variable and more difficult to estimate.
The combinations show that it is not only the individual values of \(Q\) and \(R\) that matter, but also their values relative to each other. When measurement uncertainty is high, the filter relies more on its predicted state and produces more smoothing. When process uncertainty is high, the filter becomes more responsive and places more weight on the observations.
The results from one simulation can also be affected by random variation. A Monte Carlo study is therefore used to make a more reliable comparison.

title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
Scenario 3: Monte Carlo Study
The individual scenarios are based on randomly generated data, meaning that the results from one simulation may not represent what normally happens under the same values of \(Q\) and \(R\).
A function is created to repeat the simulation and compare the Kalman filter with the moving average.


Click to expand code
run_replication <- function(n, Q, R, ma_window = 5){
  
  sim <- simulate_state(
    n = n,
    Q = Q,
    R = R
  )
  
  kf <- kalman_filt(
    y = sim$Observation,
    Q = Q,
    R = R,
    m0 = 0,
    P0 = 1
  )
  
  ma <- slide_dbl(
    sim$Observation,
    mean,
    .before = ma_window - 1,
    .complete = TRUE
  )
  
  # Same evaluation period for both methods
  valid <- !is.na(ma)
  
  data.frame(
    KF_RMSE = RMSE(
      sim$True_State[valid],
      kf$Filtered_State[valid]
    ),
    
    MA_RMSE = RMSE(
      sim$True_State[valid],
      ma[valid]
    )
  )
}


A total of 500 simulations are run for every combination of \(Q\) and \(R\).


Click to expand code
set.seed(432)

B <- 500

mc_results <- data.frame()

for(i in 1:nrow(scenario_grid)){
  
  Q_i <- scenario_grid$Q[i]
  R_i <- scenario_grid$R[i]
  
  for(b in 1:B){
    
    res <- run_replication(
      n = 250,
      Q = Q_i,
      R = R_i
    )
    
    temp <- data.frame(
      Replication = b,
      Q = Q_i,
      R = R_i,
      KF_RMSE = res$KF_RMSE,
      MA_RMSE = res$MA_RMSE
    )
    
    mc_results <- rbind(mc_results, temp)
  }
}


The results are summarised using the average RMSE, standard deviation and the percentage of simulations where the Kalman filter performs better than the moving average.


Click to expand code
mc_summary <- mc_results |>
  group_by(Q, R) |>
  summarise(
    Mean_KF_RMSE = mean(KF_RMSE),
    SD_KF_RMSE = sd(KF_RMSE),
    
    Mean_MA_RMSE = mean(MA_RMSE),
    SD_MA_RMSE = sd(MA_RMSE),
    
    KF_Better_Percent =
      mean(KF_RMSE < MA_RMSE) * 100,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

The results show that the average RMSE changes across the different uncertainty combinations. Scenarios with higher levels of uncertainty generally have larger estimation errors because there is more noise in the observations, more variation in the underlying state, or both.
The standard deviation of the RMSE also tends to become larger in scenarios with greater uncertainty, showing that estimation performance becomes more variable as the problem becomes more difficult.
The percentage of simulations where the Kalman filter has a lower RMSE than the moving average gives a clearer comparison between the two methods. This shows how consistently the Kalman filter performs better rather than relying on only one simulated dataset.
The Monte Carlo results therefore provide a more reliable view of Kalman filter performance under the different uncertainty conditions.

title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
Scenario 4: Misspecified Uncertainty
The previous scenarios assume that the Kalman filter knows the correct values of \(Q\) and \(R\). In reality, these values may not always be known correctly. This scenario looks at what happens when the uncertainty assumed by the Kalman filter is different from the true uncertainty used to generate the data.

Misspecified Measurement Uncertainty
The true measurement uncertainty is set to (R=10), while the filter is given assumed values of 1, 10 and 50.

Q_true <- 2
R_true <- 10

  n = 250,
  Q = Q_true,
  R = R_true
)

R_assumed <- c(1, 10, 50)

misspec_R_results <- data.frame()

for(R_a in R_assumed){
  
  kf <- kalman_filt(
    y = sim$Observation,
    Q = Q_true,
    R = R_a,
    m0 = 0,
    P0 = 1
  )
  
  temp <- data.frame(
    R_True = R_true,
    R_Assumed = R_a,
    RMSE = RMSE(
      sim$True_State,
      kf$Filtered_State
    ),
    Mean_Gain = mean(kf$Kalman_Gain)
  )
  
  misspec_R_results <- rbind(
    misspec_R_results,
    temp
  )
}

  knitr::kable(

When the assumed value of \(R\) is lower than the true value, the filter believes that the observations are more reliable than they actually are. This leads to a larger Kalman gain and causes the filter to place too much weight on noisy observations.
When the assumed value of \(R\) is higher than the true value, the Kalman gain becomes smaller. The filter believes that the observations are less reliable and therefore places more weight on its predicted state, resulting in more smoothing.
The results show that incorrectly specifying measurement uncertainty affects both the Kalman gain and the accuracy of the estimates.

The Kalman gain increases as the assumed value of \(Q\) increases. A larger assumed \(Q\) tells the filter that there is more uncertainty in the movement of the underlying state, so it becomes more responsive to new observations.
When \(Q\) is underestimated, the filter assumes that the true state is more stable than it actually is. This can result in too much smoothing and make the filter slower to respond to changes.
When \(Q\) is overestimated, the filter assumes that the state changes more than it actually does. It therefore places more weight on new observations and may become too responsive to noise.
