title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
Scenario 5: Structural Change
A structural change is introduced at (t=100), where the true state experiences a permanent shift of 15 units.


Click to expand code
simulate_break <- function(
    n,
    Q,
    R,
    break_point = 100,
    break_size = 15,
    x0 = 0){
  
  xt = numeric(n)
  yt = numeric(n)
  
  xt[1] = x0
  
  for(i in 2:n){
    
    wt = rnorm(
      1,
      mean = 0,
      sd = sqrt(Q)
    )
    
    xt[i] = xt[i - 1] + wt
    
    # Permanent level shift
    if(i == break_point){
      xt[i] <- xt[i] + break_size
    }
  }
  
  for(i in 1:n){
    yt[i] = xt[i] +
      rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(R))
  }
  
  data.frame(
    Time = 1:n,
    True_State = xt,
    Observation = yt
  )
}




Click to expand code
set.seed(432)

break_sim <- simulate_break(
  n = 250,
  Q = 2,
  R = 1.5,
  break_point = 100,
  break_size = 15
)

break_kf <- kalman_filt(
  y = break_sim$Observation,
  Q = 2,
  R = 1.5,
  m0 = 0,
  P0 = 1
)


The response of the Kalman filter to the change is shown below.


Click to expand code
break_data <- data.frame(
  Time = 1:250,
  True_State = break_sim$True_State,
  Observation = break_sim$Observation,
  Filtered_State = break_kf$Filtered_State
)

ggplot(break_data, aes(x = Time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Observation),
            alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = True_State, colour = "green"),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Filtered_State, colour = "blue"),
            linewidth = 1,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 100,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Kalman Filter Response to a Sudden State Change",
    subtitle = "Structural change at t = 100",
    x = "Time",
    y = "State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Recovery is defined as the point where the estimation error becomes less than 10% of the size of the structural change.


Click to expand code
break_point <- 100
break_size <- 15
tolerance <- 0.10 * abs(break_size)

post_break_error <- abs(
  break_sim$True_State[break_point:250] -
  break_kf$Filtered_State[break_point:250]
)

first_recovered <- which(
  post_break_error <= tolerance
)[1]

recovery_time <- first_recovered - 1

recovery_time


[1] 1


The filter was able to adjust relatively quickly to the change. Under the values of \(Q\) and \(R\) used in this simulation, the recovery time was one observation.
This does not mean that the Kalman filter will always recover from a structural change within one observation. The recovery time depends on the size of the change, the values of \(Q\) and \(R\), and the definition used to determine when the filter has recovered.
The result does show the importance of the trade-off between smoothing and responsiveness. A filter that produces very smooth estimates may work well when the process is stable but may take longer to adjust when a real change occurs.

title: State Estimation Under Uncertainty: A Simulation Study of the Kalman Filter
text:
Scenario 6: Missing Observations
Missing observations are introduced at rates of 0%, 10%, 25% and 40% to see how they affect the Kalman filter.
The Kalman filter is changed slightly so that when an observation is missing, the prediction step is still completed but the measurement update is skipped.


Click to expand code
kalman_filt_missing <- function(y, Q, R, m0, P0){
  
  N = length(y)
  
  at = numeric(N)
  Rt = numeric(N)
  Qt = rep(NA_real_, N)
  mt = numeric(N)
  Pt = numeric(N)
  et = rep(NA_real_, N)
  Kt = rep(NA_real_, N)
  
  for(i in 1:N){
    
    # Prediction
    if(i == 1){
      at[i] = m0
      Rt[i] = P0 + Q
    } else {
      at[i] = mt[i - 1]
      Rt[i] = Pt[i - 1] + Q
    }
    
    if(is.na(y[i])){
      
      # No measurement:
      # prediction becomes filtered estimate
      mt[i] = at[i]
      Pt[i] = Rt[i]
      
    } else {
      
      # Normal measurement update
      et[i] = y[i] - at[i]
      Qt[i] = Rt[i] + R
      
      Kt[i] = Rt[i] / Qt[i]
      
      mt[i] = at[i] +
        Kt[i] * et[i]
      
      Pt[i] = (1 - Kt[i]) * Rt[i]
    }
  }
  
  data.frame(
    Time = 1:N,
    Observation = y,
    Predicted_State = at,
    Prediction_Variance = Rt,
    Innovation = et,
    Innovation_Variance = Qt,
    Kalman_Gain = Kt,
    Filtered_State = mt,
    Filtered_Variance = Pt
  )
}


The different percentages of missing observations are then tested.


Click to expand code
set.seed(432)

missing_rates <- c(0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40)

missing_results <- data.frame()

for(rate in missing_rates){
  
  y_missing <- yt
  
  if(rate > 0){
    
    missing_index <- sample(
      1:n,
      size = round(n * rate),
      replace = FALSE
    )
    
    y_missing[missing_index] <- NA
  }
  
  kf <- kalman_filt_missing(
    y = y_missing,
    Q = Q,
    R = R,
    m0 = 0,
    P0 = 1
  )
  
  temp <- data.frame(
    Time = 1:n,
    True_State = xt,
    Observation = y_missing,
    Filtered_State = kf$Filtered_State,
    Filtered_Variance = kf$Filtered_Variance,
    Missing_Rate = rate
  )
  
  missing_results <- rbind(
    missing_results,
    temp
  )
}




Click to expand code
missing_summary <- missing_results |>
  group_by(Missing_Rate) |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = RMSE(
      True_State,
      Filtered_State
    ),
    Mean_Uncertainty =
      mean(Filtered_Variance)
  )

missing_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Effect of missing observations on Kalman filter performance"
  )

The results show that having more missing observations leads to less accurate estimates, with RMSE generally increasing as the percentage of missing values increases. Mean uncertainty also becomes larger as more observations are removed.
The Kalman filter can still produce an estimate when an observation is missing because it can continue with the prediction step. However, without an observation, it cannot use the normal measurement update to correct the prediction. The uncertainty therefore increases until new observations become available.
This shows that the Kalman filter is able to handle missing observations, but the certainty of its estimates is affected when less information is available.

title: arch garch lab
text:
Problem 2

a) Which ARMA/GARCH model is being fit? Write down the model using the same parameter names as in the R output.
The model being fit at the end of problem 1 is a ARMA(1,0)/GARCH(1,0) model which is made of an AR(1) process for the conditional mean and an ARCH(1) process for the conditional variance.
The maean equation is given as: \[y_t = \mu + ar1 \cdot y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t\]
And the variance equation is given as: \[\sigma_t^2 = \omega + alpha1 \cdot \epsilon_{t-1}^2\]
Where:

\(y_t\): The differenced T-bill series (Del.Tbill) at time \(t\).
\(\mu\) (mu): The constant in the mean equation.
\(ar1\) (ar1): The autoregressive coefficient for the first lag.
\(\epsilon_t\): The error term at time \(t\) (where \(\epsilon_t = z_t \sigma_t\) and \(z_t \sim N(0,1)\)).
\(\sigma_t^2\): The conditional variance at time \(t\).
\(\omega\) (omega): The constant in the variance equation.
\(alpha1\) (alpha1): The ARCH coefficient capturing the effect of the lagged squared error.



b) What are the estimates of each of the parameters in the model?

title: arch garch lab
text:
Problem 3

a) Describe what is plotted by acf(res). What, if anything, does the plot tell you about the fit of the model?
The autocorrelation function of the ordinary residuals is plotted from the fitted model and helps identify if the fitted model successfully captures the linear dependence. The dataset show only a significant lag at 0 but besides that lag 1 appears significant my only just.


b) Describe what is plotted by acf(res^2). What, if anything, does the plot tell you about the fit of the model?
The autocorrelation function of the squared raw residuals. and it captures the presence of volatility clustering in the residuals. There are few significant lags which indicate conditional heteroskedasticity remains.


c) Describe what is plotted by acf(res_std^2). What, if anything, does the plot tell you about the fit of the model?
The autocorrelation function of the squared standardized residuals is plotted to evaluate whether the fitted GARCH model successfully captured the time-varying volatility. Based on the ACF of Std Res^2 plot, the GARCH(1,0) model successfully eliminated most of the volatility clustering seen in the raw squared residuals. However, a few minor significant lags still slightly exceed the confidence bounds. This suggests that while the current model is a vast improvement, a higher-order GARCH model might be needed to capture the remaining traces of conditional heteroskedasticity perfectly.


d) What is contained in the the variable garch.model.Tbill@sigma.t?
This variable contains the time series of the estimated conditional standard deviations (\(\sigma_t\)) generated by the fitted model. It extracts the actual point-by-point volatility measurements that the model calculated for the dataset over time.


e) Is there anything noteworthy in the plot produced by the code plot(res_std)?
The plot of the standardized residuals shows that the variance has been successfully stabilized over time. While the raw residuals had a large amount of volatility between index 100 and 150, the standardized residuals show this volatility clustering has been flattened out, with the residuals oscillating much more evenly between -3 and 3. This seems to show that the model effectively captured the conditional heteroskedasticity.

Similarly, the ACF plot of the squared standardized residuals shows no significant lags, confirming that the GARCH(1,1) component effectively accounted for the volatility clustering and conditional heteroskedasticity. Problem definition: Define the specific objective, which is forecasting the future sales volume for the manufacturer’s various biscuit products. Model validation: Evaluate how accurately the chosen models predict future sales before relying on them. Question 3








Time Series Plot
ACF Plot
Reasoning




1. Daily morning temperature of a cow
B
The series wanders randomly without a distinct repeating period. ACF B matches this by showing a slow, smooth decay, which is typical for highly autocorrelated data with no seasonality.


2. Accidental deaths in USA (monthly)
A
There is a strong, consistent monthly seasonality but no overall trend. ACF A shows this stationary seasonal pattern perfectly, with clear spikes every 12 lags.


3. International airline passengers
D
The plot shows a strong upward trend combined with monthly seasonality. ACF D matches this because the strong trend causes the ACF to decay very slowly overall, while the seasonality creates the small bumps along the decay.


4. Annual mink trappings (Canada)
C
This series exhibits a long cycle (roughly 10 years between peaks) rather than fixed monthly seasonality. ACF C reflects this cyclical behavior, as the autocorrelation oscillates and peaks around lag 10.

Question 6
A classic example of a non-stationary series is the daily closing IBM stock prices.Figure 3 shows the analysis of n = 369 daily closing prices for IBM stock. Explain how eachplot shows the series is non-stationary and should be differenced.
The first plot shows periods of high closing prices followed by periods of low closing prices, wandering without a stable baseline, which indicates the mean is not constant over time. The ACF plot shows persistence in the effect of past lags on the current price value, with the spikes decaying very slowly rather than quickly dropping to zero. This slow decay confirms the series is non-stationary. Finally, the PACF plot shows almost a 1 autocorrelation with the previous closing price, meaning that the current price is heavily based on the previous day’s closing price. Together, these plots show the series closely follows a random walk and needs to be differenced to make it stationary.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Spectral analysis looks at a time series in terms of its frequencies. This helps identify repeating patterns that may be less obvious from the time plot alone.
Show R code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

title: Spectral analysis
section: Frequency, period and R’s frequency argument
text:
Frequency, period and R’s frequency argument
Following the notes, use m for period in observations, f=1/m for cycles per observation and \omega=2\pi f for radians per observation. The Nyquist limit is f_N=1/2. R’s ts(..., frequency = 12) describes 12 observations per time unit, which is appropriate for monthly observations indexed in years; it does not set f=12.


Show R code
units <- data.frame(example = c("Monthly annual cycle", "Quarterly annual cycle",
                               "Hourly daily cycle", "Daily weekly cycle"),
                    period = c(12, 4, 24, 7)) |>
  mutate(f = 1 / period, omega = 2 * pi * f)
units


                 example period          f     omega
1   Monthly annual cycle     12 0.08333333 0.5235988
2 Quarterly annual cycle      4 0.25000000 1.5707963
3     Hourly daily cycle     24 0.04166667 0.2617994
4     Daily weekly cycle      7 0.14285714 0.8975979


For consistency, the helper below deliberately converts inputs to plain numeric vectors. Every plotted frequency is therefore cycles per observation, regardless of a ts object’s time scale. To convert monthly results to cycles per year, multiply the frequency by 12. A spectral density must also be divided by 12 when changing that horizontal scale if its integrated power is to stay the same.


Show R code
spectrum_df <- function(x, spans = NULL, taper = 0.1, detrend = TRUE,
                        pad = 0, fast = FALSE) {
  s = spec.pgram(as.numeric(x), spans = spans, taper = taper,
                  detrend = detrend, demean = !detrend,
                  pad = pad, fast = fast, plot = FALSE)
  data.frame(frequency = as.numeric(s$freq), power = as.numeric(s$spec))
}

plot_spectrum <- function(d, title = NULL) {
  ggplot(d, aes(frequency, pmax(power, .Machine$double.eps))) +
    geom_line(colour = "steelblue") + scale_y_log10() +
    labs(x = "Frequency (cycles per observation)",
         y = "Spectral ordinate (log scale)", title = title)
}

top_peaks <- function(d, number = 5) {
  # Local maxima, so a broad peak is not reported as five adjacent frequencies.
  k = which(d$power > c(-Inf, head(d$power, -1)) &
               d$power >= c(tail(d$power, -1), -Inf))
  d[k, ] |> arrange(desc(power)) |> slice_head(n = number) |>
    mutate(period_observations = 1 / frequency)
}


A frequency of 0.2 gives a period of 5 quarters, or 1.25 years, and an angular frequency of 0.4\pi radians per observation. To study a weekly cycle, the sampling interval needs to be less than 3.5 days. Daily observations would be a useful choice.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Compute the raw periodogram yourself
For centered values x_t, calculate I_j=|\sum_t x_t e^{-2\pi ijt/n}|^2/n. We retain positive frequencies. This is the two-sided-density convention restricted to the positive grid, matching spec.pgram() with preprocessing switched off. Other books use a factor of two or 2\pi; compare definitions before comparing ordinates.


Show R code
raw_periodogram <- function(x) {
  x = as.numeric(x) - mean(x)
  n = length(x)
  j = seq_len(floor(n / 2))
  data.frame(frequency = j / n, power = Mod(fft(x)[j + 1])^2 / n)
}

set.seed(24)
n <- 240
t <- seq_len(n)
wave <- 2 * cos(2*pi*t/24) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.7)
ggplot(data.frame(t, wave), aes(t, wave)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Value")









Show R code
manual <- raw_periodogram(wave)
builtin <- spectrum_df(wave, taper = 0, detrend = FALSE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(manual$power, builtin$power, tolerance = 1e-8)))
plot_spectrum(manual, "A noisy cycle with period 24") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1/24, linetype = 2)









Show R code
top_peaks(manual, 3)


   frequency      power period_observations
1 0.04166667 241.341233            24.00000
2 0.07500000   2.430989            13.33333
3 0.20000000   2.124690             5.00000


Show R code
# Parseval check: double interior positive frequencies, but not the Nyquist bin.
weights <- ifelse(abs(manual$frequency - 0.5) < 1e-12, 1, 2)
c(variance_divisor_n = mean((wave - mean(wave))^2),
  spectral_sum = sum(weights * manual$power) / n,
  R_sample_variance = var(wave))


variance_divisor_n       spectral_sum  R_sample_variance 
          2.468582           2.468582           2.478911 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(sum(weights * manual$power)/n - mean((wave - mean(wave))^2)) < 1e-8)


The finite-sample equality uses variance with divisor n; var() uses n-1. A single positive-frequency ordinate is not itself a fraction of total variance. With this convention the full frequency range, or the correctly weighted positive half, is needed.
The main peak should be near 1/24, which corresponds to a cycle every 24 observations. Increasing the noise or reducing the amplitude makes the cycle harder to identify. The estimated period may not be exact because the periodogram only evaluates a grid of frequencies. An off-grid cycle spreads its power across nearby frequencies.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Seasonal harmonics


Show R code
set.seed(61)
tm <- 1:240
seasonal_examples <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(t = tm, y = 5 * sin(2*pi*tm/12) + rnorm(240, sd = 0.2),
             pattern = "Smooth annual wave"),
  data.frame(t = tm, y = 10 * as.integer(tm %% 12 == 0) + rnorm(240, sd = 0.2),
             pattern = "One spike every December"))
season_spectra <- bind_rows(lapply(split(seasonal_examples, seasonal_examples$pattern), function(d) {
  transform(spectrum_df(d$y, taper = 0, detrend = FALSE), pattern = d$pattern[1])
}))
ggplot(season_spectra, aes(frequency, power)) + geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() + geom_vline(xintercept = (1:6)/12, linetype = 2, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~pattern) + labs(x = "Cycles per month", y = "Spectral ordinate")









Peaks at 12, 6 and 4 months can be harmonics of the same annual pattern. A sharp seasonal spike needs several frequencies to represent its shape, while a smooth annual wave is mainly represented by the annual frequency. The ACF shows repetition at seasonal lags, while the spectrum shows the frequencies contributing to that repetition.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Leakage, tapering and padding
A finite observation window spreads an off-grid sinusoid across adjacent Fourier frequencies. Tapering softens the edges, but broadens the main peak. Padding interpolates the frequency grid; it does not add observations or improve the underlying resolution.


Show R code
off_grid <- cos(2*pi*(1:120)/17.3)
leakage <- bind_rows(
  transform(spectrum_df(off_grid, taper = 0, detrend = FALSE), method = "No taper"),
  transform(spectrum_df(off_grid, taper = 0.1, detrend = FALSE), method = "10% taper"),
  transform(spectrum_df(off_grid, taper = 0.1, detrend = FALSE, pad = 4),
            method = "10% taper; padded grid"))
ggplot(leakage, aes(frequency, power)) + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1/17.3, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 1) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.02, 0.12)) +
  labs(x = "Cycles per observation", y = "Spectral ordinate")









Tapering reduces leakage away from the main peak but makes the peak wider. Padding gives a finer frequency grid, but it does not add information or resolve cycles that the sample is too short to separate. Sampling can also cause aliasing: frequencies above the Nyquist limit of 0.5 cycles per observation can appear as lower frequencies.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Smoothing and interpreting peaks
The raw periodogram is noisy, even for a long series. Smoothing reduces this variability, but too much smoothing can hide narrow peaks or merge nearby cycles.


Show R code
set.seed(71)
ar2 <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = c(1.5, -0.75)), n = 1024))
smoothing <- bind_rows(lapply(c(1, 9, 25), function(span) {
  transform(spectrum_df(ar2, spans = if (span == 1) NULL else span), span = span)
}))
ggplot(smoothing, aes(frequency, power)) + geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() + facet_wrap(~span) +
  labs(x = "Cycles per observation", y = "Spectral ordinate")









I would use moderate smoothing, such as span 9, as a starting point for identifying a broad peak. The larger span gives a smoother estimate but loses detail. For two close seasonal frequencies, less smoothing would be more appropriate. A broad peak can represent a stochastic cycle, so the peaks in the time plot do not have to be equally spaced.
A large peak alone does not establish seasonality. Fisher’s statistic, g=\max(I_j)/\sum I_j, tests peak concentration against a white-noise background. Rejection can also result from serial dependence, so it does not by itself prove a deterministic cycle. Trends and structural breaks can also produce low-frequency power.

title: Spectral analysis
text:
Application: monthly CO2
I remove a quadratic trend while retaining the seasonal pattern. The frequencies are measured in cycles per month.


Show R code
co2_y <- as.numeric(co2)
co2_t <- seq_along(co2_y)
co2_trend <- lm(co2_y ~ co2_t + I(co2_t^2))
co2_resid <- residuals(co2_trend)
ggplot(data.frame(t = as.numeric(time(co2)), value = co2_resid), aes(t, value)) +
  geom_line() + labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 after quadratic detrending")









Show R code
co2_spec <- spectrum_df(co2_resid, spans = 3, detrend = FALSE)
plot_spectrum(co2_spec, "Detrended monthly CO2") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = (1:6)/12, linetype = 2, alpha = 0.3)









Show R code
top_peaks(co2_spec)


    frequency      power period_observations
1 0.083333333 430.121569            12.00000
2 0.166666667  31.898296             6.00000
3 0.002136752  29.228427           468.00000
4 0.014957265   3.715764            66.85714
5 0.023504274   3.264900            42.54545




Show R code
acf(co2_resid, lag.max = 36, main = "ACF of detrended monthly CO2")









The annual cycle corresponds to f=1/12, giving a period of 12 months. Peaks near 2/12 and 3/12 would represent harmonics with periods of 6 and 4 months. These can describe the shape of the same annual pattern. The time plot and ACF provide a useful check on the seasonal interpretation.
Removing the trend helps separate long-term growth from seasonality. If I also removed the fitted seasonal component, I would be checking for remaining cycles in the residuals. Seasonal differencing at lag 12 also removes power at the annual frequency and its harmonics, so it would change the question being investigated.

title: Exponential Smoothing prac
text:
Show R code
# library for the dataset
library(fpp2)

dat_q1 <- marathon 

# function for simple exponential smoothing
simp_ets <- function(y, alpha, level){
  n = length(y)
  yhat = numeric(n)
  yhat[1] = level
  
  for (i in 2:n){
    yhat[i] = alpha * y[i-1] + (1 - alpha) * yhat[i-1]
  }
  
  next_fc = alpha * y[n] + (1 - alpha) * yhat[n]
  
  return(list(forecast = next_fc, fitted = yhat))
}

# fitted using the ses function
fit <- ses(y = dat_q1, h = 1)

# optimal values extracted for mine
res <- simp_ets(y = dat_q1, alpha = fit$model$par[1], level = fit$model$par[2])

# comparison using a data frame to display as a table
data.frame(
  My_Forecast = res$forecast, 
  SES_Forecast = as.numeric(fit$mean)
)


      My_Forecast SES_Forecast
alpha    130.3563     130.3563


Yes the values are the same





Show R code
# for the manual prediction intervals
sig <- sd(dat_q1 - fit$fitted)
pi_l_manual <- res$forecast - 1.96 * sig
pi_u_manual <- res$forecast + 1.96 * sig

# using ses
fit_pi <- ses(y = dat_q1, h = 1, level = 95)
pi_l_ses <- fit_pi$lower[1]
pi_u_ses <- fit_pi$upper[1]

data.frame(
  Method = c("Manual", "ses() Function"),
  Forecast = c(res$forecast, as.numeric(fit_pi$mean)),
  Lower_PI = c(pi_l_manual, pi_l_ses),
  Upper_PI = c(pi_u_manual, pi_u_ses)
)


              Method Forecast Lower_PI Upper_PI
alpha         Manual 130.3563 119.7273 140.9854
      ses() Function 130.3563 119.5394 141.1733


I think they are off a bit because I used 1.96.





Show R code
autoplot(dat_q1, series = "Data") +
  autolayer(fit$fitted, series = "Fitted") +
  ggtitle("Boston Marathon Winning Times with SES Fitted Values") +
  ylab("Minutes") + xlab("Year")









The fit seems to be quite bad. Its not able to capture much variation in the data

Question 2
Consider the oil series (annual oil production in Saudi Arabia, in library fpp2). Use the ses() function in R to find the optimal values of 𝛼 and ℓ0, and generate forecasts for the next four years. Compute a 95% prediction interval for the first forecast using 𝑦̂±1.96×𝑠, where 𝑠 is the standard deviation of the residuals. Compare your interval with the interval produced by R.

title: Exponential Smoothing prac
text:
Question 3


Show R code
ses_sse <- function(par, y) {
  alpha = par[1]
  level = par[2]
  
  n = length(y)
  y_hat = numeric(n)
  y_hat[1] = level
  
  for (i in 2:n) {
    y_hat[i] = alpha * y[i-1] + (1 - alpha) * y_hat[i-1]
  }
  
  errors = y - y_hat
  return(sum(errors^2)) # returns SSE
}

oil_subset <- window(oil, start=1996, end=2013)


opt_res <- optim(par = c(0.5, oil_subset[1]), 
                 fn = ses_sse, 
                 y = oil_subset,
                 method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(0, -Inf),
                 upper = c(1, Inf))



# ses()
fit_oil_sub <- ses(oil_subset, h=1)

data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Alpha", "Initial Level (l0)"),
  Manual_optim = c(opt_res$par[1], opt_res$par[2]),
  SES_function = c(as.numeric(fit_oil_sub$model$par["alpha"]), as.numeric(fit_oil_sub$model$par["l"]))
)


           Parameter Manual_optim SES_function
1              Alpha    0.8338438    0.8338901
2 Initial Level (l0)  446.5754462  446.5867935

title: Exponential Smoothing prac
text:
Question 5
Simulate data using the state-space model formulation of simple exponential smoothing (and Holt’s exponential smoothing if you want). Then estimate the parameters using optim, and the R functions.


Show R code
# function for ses for exponential smoothing
simulate_ses <- function(n, alpha, l0, sigma) {
  y = numeric(n)
  l = numeric(n)
  e = rnorm(n, 0, sigma)
  
  l[1] = l0
  y[1] = l[1] + e[1] 
  
  for(t in 2:n) {
    y[t] = l[t-1] + e[t]           
    l[t] = l[t-1] + alpha * e[t]    
  }
  
  return(ts(y))
}

# simulating data
set.seed(123)
sim_data <- simulate_ses(n=100, alpha=0.3, l0=10, sigma=1)

# finding optimal values
sim_opt <- optim(par = c(0.5, sim_data[1]), 
                 fn = ses_sse, 
                 y = sim_data,
                 method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(0, -Inf),
                 upper = c(1, Inf))


opt_alpha <- sim_opt$par[1]
opt_l0 <- sim_opt$par[2]

data.frame(
  Source = c("True Parameters", "Manual optim()"),
  Alpha = c(0.3, opt_alpha),
  Initial_Level_l0 = c(10, opt_l0)
)


           Source     Alpha Initial_Level_l0
1 True Parameters 0.3000000         10.00000
2  Manual optim() 0.2746831         10.33156


relatively close to the true parameter value
